subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has given the Chair notice of a question of privilege and also advised the Chair that there seems to be some disposition in the House that the question of privilege is of such a nature that it ought to be taken forthwith.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleagues with respect to this matter. I regret very much that it is necessary to deal with this question on a day set aside for the discussion of pollution and its effects on native people. Therefore, I shall be very brief with respect to this matter.
Mr. Auguste Choquette is quoted as saying before an open court and I quote:
-if everyone who had ever taken or given $600 or $700 bribes in their life were arrested, 50 per cent of the MP's would no longer be sitting.
He also said:
I know it because I was an MP for five years.
Clearly, he means MP's performing as members of parliament.
The source of these remarks and the wide distribution they have been given forces our attention. An institution as venal and corrupted as Mr. Choquette asserts this parliament to be would have no right to respect from the Canadian people. If true, the remarks must be acted upon and the historical penalties exacted; if they are false, a public declaration by Mr. Choquette must be made withdrawing the slanderous accusations against half the members sitting here.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext:
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the remarks are almost certainly a question of privilege. Standing Order 76 and Beauchesne citations 434, 435 and 108(5) deal directly with bribery. The last citation calls the offering of a bribe "an insult not only to the member himself, but to the House"; and the acceptance of a bribe has always been "a grave offence, which has been visited by the severest punishments". On page 138 of May's 18th edition, the penalty described is imprisonment or expulsion from the House.
Acceptance of a bribe is a serious form of corruption and Beauchesne 111(h) states that "imputations against members of corruption in the execution of their duties" is a breach of privilege. Citation 110, in describing "high violations" against the House, provides:
The same rule applies to a charge against a member for conduct which renders him unworthy to sit in Parliament and to criticize the House for not expelling him.
So gross an accusation, Mr. Speaker, must surely be justified with facts, or apologized for at the bar of the Hoilse.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext:
It seems to me important that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections examine Mr. Choquette and establish the facts for the sake of the reputation of parliament and all its members. I therefore move:
That the accusation that a substantial proportion of the members of the House of Commons have been in receipt of bribes be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I eagerly support the comments of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I am certain, for that matter, that all members of the House will agree with me. Mr. Speaker, like all members I was appalled at the report of Mr. Choquette's statement.

It is essential, and no one will question, that the integrity of all members of this House be protected. It is with that thought in mind that I fully support the motion made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker).
speakername: Mr.   J.-J. Blais@Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are all pleased that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has raised this important issue at the first opportunity. I think both he and the previous speaker are to be commended for the brevity of their remarks. It seems to me that the case is so clear that it does not need extensive debate. I hope that Your Honour will find there is a prima facie case of privilege and that the motion made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton will therefore be ruled in order.
We all feel that when someone like our former colleague, Mr. Auguste Choquette, makes a statement of this kind, especially when he makes it in open court, he should be called upon to answer for it, to substantiate it or to withdraw the serious charges he has made. I hope that very shortly this matter will be before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I should like to echo
something the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) said the

May 7, 1976
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
other day in another connection, and that is that when things like this are said, or when improper things are done, it is not just one party in the House or a few individuals here, but it is the whole institution of parliament that comes under a shadow. It is really serious that there is such cynicism in Canada, as there is today, about this institution and about democracy, and we should be taking the most positive steps we can to correct this situation. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I indicate our readiness to support the motion that has been presented to you this morning.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the motion which has just been presented should be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections because, on the one hand, if false allegations have been made, I think it is the interest of all members to protect themselves; this is the only way they can protect themselves; and on the other hand, if the allegations are true, the public will know what is going on in Parliament. I for one am very satisfied with the motion, and I think that we must clarify all these allegations coming from all sides and all these so-called bribes we hear about every day. It would be one of the first opportunities for the Committee on Privileges and Elections to shed some light on these matters, and if it is successful in doing so, we will have to continue. That is why I am in favour of this motion.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should just like to add one word. I endorse the motion, but I want to emphasize something that may have been said in order to make it very clear. Traditionally, we in Canada have had very dedicated men and women in our public service, and traditionally they have been known as people of high integrity. As I read the statement, if it is correctly reported, it is not only a slight on every member of parliament, as well as every person who has been a member, but also a slight on the dedicated people in the public service of Canada.

subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext:
Order, please. For very obvious reasons it is clear that the motion enjoys widespread, if not unanimous, support, and I would be surprised if it were not unanimous. If the Chair were to have any hesitation in putting the question at this time it would only be in respect of the ironing out of procedural difficulties which might be involved. I do not see why that cannot be done in a preliminary way by the committee, if in fact the matter were to be referred there.
For example, in respect of the motion it does occur to me that some reflection should occur, until perhaps later in the day or until Monday, regarding the form of the motion itself and other paragraphs that may be added. I wish to make it very clear that there is not the slightest doubt in the Chair's mind that the question ought to be put to the House. After all, it should be stressed that a decision which is made by the Chair is often referred to as a decision as to whether or not a prima facie question of privilege exists. That is a convenient phrase, but the fact of the matter is that it is not entirely correct. What the Chair is doing is

simply making a decision as to whether the proceedings ought to be stopped in order to give priority to a motion which has been raised under the title of a question of privilege. There is not the slightest doubt in the Chair's mind that this ought to be done either now or at an appropriate time.
The only reason I suggest a time lag before putting the question is that there are things to be considered as, for example, the language of the motion, which obviously had to be prepared very hurriedly, and, secondly, the powers the committee ought to enjoy, as well as the other powers the House may wish to exercise in respect of this sort of thing. After all, this is a statement not made by a member over whom the House has some jurisdiction, but a statement made by someone outside. It may be necessary that the House exercise some special powers in that regard. It may also be that there may be some conflict with some privileges of a lawyer pleading a case in open court; I do not know. However, it occurs to me that the Chair ought to make clear, and I now wish to do so, that I am prepared to interrupt the proceedings now to put this question or I am prepared to give the House a bit of time to reflect on the polishing of the motion, only from a procedural point of view, to make sure that after reflection the motion in fact does include all the powers the committee ought to enjoy to investigate a matter of that sort. I would appreciate some guidance from the members in that respect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ME. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. AUGUSTE CHOQUETTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what you have said and I think, having regard to the importance of the question, it would be the wish of all members of the House that the committee be completely empowered having regard to the subject matter or empowered to the extent it can be. I for one, as the mover of the motion, would certainly have no objection. I hope those who spoke in support of it and the members of the House generally would have no objection to the delay for the reasons you suggested.

Mr. Speaker, I have one brief supplementary for the Prime Minister. In his address to the Law of the Sea Conference on April 8, Dr. Kissinger said that if the deep seabeds are not subject to international agreement, the United States can and will proceed to explore and mine on its own. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. On May 3, in the minister's absence I directed a question to his parliamentary secretary regarding the five strains of polio virus which had been found in two sewage treatment plants in the Ottawa area. I asked whether these virus samples had been sent to the biology laboratory. The parliamentary secretary stated they had just been sent and that no report had been received. I now want to ask the minister two questions. First, can he tell us whether the report of the biology lab has been received and whether these strains are suspect-ible to Salk vaccine? Second, why, since the department knew of this since last January, were these tests not made at an earlier date.

subtopic: POLIO VIRUS IN OTTAWA AREA-SUSCEPTIBILITY OF STRAIN TO SALK VACCINE-REASON FOR DELAY IN TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the data relating to the 15 polio viruses that were isolated in the Ottawa area were reported at the symposium held at the University of Ottawa on January 23, 1976 at which were present officials from the local health authority, the Ontario health authority, and the federal government. Our report to the University of Ottawa indicated that ten of the 15 polio viruses were classified as vaccine-like. The remaining five strains showed no reaction with Sabin vaccine anti-serum, but could not be characterized, I repeat, could not be characterized as virulent strains. I am advised that it is rather difficult to establish the origin of the five polio virus strains, but the polio virus is a relatively stable one. Therefore, immunization with either Sabin or Salk vaccine would be quite adequate to meet the problem in this instance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member, being a layman in the field like myself, will not want to create undue fears vis-a-vis the effectiveness of the existing vaccine in Canada. I might advise him that the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents met last October 30 and 31 to study the matter of all vaccines presently used in Canada, and proposed an immunization schedule. Both Sabin and Salk vaccines were found suitable to fight polio. They are both acceptable ways of treating polio. With regard to these particular strains that have been identified, I am advised that there is no reason to doubt that either vaccine would be adequate to combat them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the interval that has just been broken by this "friendly" exchange there have been discussions among representatives of the parties respecting the form the motion should take. I think I should say at the outset that all of us are extremely grateful for the assistance of the parliamentary counsel and the officers at the table with respect to this matter.
We considered the possibility of expanding the motion in a detailed way, but it was decided that perhaps that ought not to be done, that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections had sufficient powers and that if they required any additional powers in order satisfactorily to deal with the matter, they could return to the House. I am satisfied the temper and mood of the House in respect of this matter is such that those powers would be given willingly.
If Your Honour finds this motion acceptable, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker), has in a preliminary way moved with the greatest speed and I am sure all hon. members are grateful to him for the speed and interest he has shown in this matter.
The upshot of our discussions is that I would suggest to Your Honour a motion which, if it could be, would be seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) but which, for our purposes, will in fact be seconded by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais). I would move:
That the alleged accusation by Mr. Auguste Choquette that a substantial number of the members of the House of Commons have been in receipt of bribes be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
I hope you will find that motion acceptable, sir.

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS AND STANDING ORDERS

speechtext:
1. Total costs to the Government of Canada for programs related to the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1972, estimated to the end of 1975-76, were $280,138,000. This figure includes estimated government expenditures of $2,612,419 incurred through the International Joint Commission during the same period.
2.	(a) 1971-72: $31,331,000, (b) 1972-73: $38,928,000, (c) 1973-74: $84,289,000, (d) 1974-75: $66,835,000, (e) 1975-76: $58,755,000.
3.	The Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement was signed on April 15, 1972. The agreement specifies that it is to remain in force for a period of five years and thereafter until terminated upon twelve months notice being given in writing by either party. It further specifies that programs directed to the achievement of its water quality objectives be either completed or in the process of implementation by December 31, 1975. That date is not however a termination date but rather specifies a target date for certain activities. The process of cleaning up the Great Lakes is inevitably a
long one, and the IJC, in its Third Annual Report on Great Lakes Water Quality, speaks of a decade or more before the goals of the Agreement can be fully realized.
4.	No. Given the nature of the challenge and the indefinite time frame, it is impossible to estimate the total costs involved to all the governments concerned. Future costs will depend on the degree wo which the parties respond to ongoing recommendations of the International Joint Commission in respect of activities necessary to achieve the objectives of the agreement.
5.	The government is satisfied that the United States is making a sincere effort to live up to its commitments. Despite some delay in early implementation of United States programs, action has now been taken by the United States authorities to accelerate activities required to meet the objectives of the agreement.
6.	According to information provided by United States authorities, the total expenditure to 1975 is $2,353,000,000. This figure represents only costs to the United States government. By years: (a) $225,000,000; (b) $419,000,000; (c) $509,000,000; (d) $900,000,000.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS AND STANDING ORDERS
subsubtopic: OPERATION AND EFFICIENCY OF RAILWAY PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Transport Canada advises as follows: 1. As part of the Railway Passenger Program announced on January 29, the railways and the government are now preparing plans for the improvement of corridor services of which the Ottawa-Montreal route forms a part. Some changes will be announced by CN in the April timetable. An announcement on a corridor demonstration project is to be made in the near future. Public hearings on the Montreal-Maritimes service will be conducted by the CTC and will be completed by late 1977. These hearings will follow a similar format to those now underway on the Montreal-Vancouver trans-continental services, permitting the public to comment on and provide inputs to the developments of future plans for these services.
2.	In reviewing the Montreal-Maritimes services the views of all interested parties, including the Members of Parliament from the region will be sought. I would be pleased to receive the suggestions of the Honourable Members on these Maritime services. The Management of Canadian National Railways advises as follows:
3.	The quality of work done in the Railway's shops has been and is of a high standard. Canadian National does not normally compete against private industry in the solicitation of work for its shops. Every effort has been made this year to introduce work of a railway nature into the shops to help minimize the effect of lay-offs. A major passenger car upgrading program was approved early in 1976 and, although passenger work is not performed in Moncton,
Order Paper Questions
that shop did benefit because of the need to offload freight car work from other railway shops.
4.	(a) The frequency of inspection varies according to the class of track but generally: 1. Track is inspected so that not more than two calendar days elapse between inspections. These regular inspections are performed by an experienced employee riding on a track motor car or Hy-rail car, at slow speed. The Roadmaster must make at least one of these inspections each week. 2. Twice a year a walking inspection must be made. One of these inspections must be made by the Roadmaster; the other must be made by the Track Foreman. 3. Once every three weeks during summer conditions and once every week during winter conditions the track ride quality must be checked by riding a train. These train inspections must be done by a Roadmaster. 4. If there are conditions anticipated, such as earth slides, floods, extremely high or low temperatures, forest fire hazard and vandalism, track is inspected more frequently. (b) and (c) CTC regulations require mandatory and operational inspections of all rail equipment prior to being released for service. These regulations are further augmented by Company developed inspection procedures. These requirements are of a continuous, trip and periodic nature and are so designed to ensure that all critical rail equipment components are thoroughly inspected within a predetermined period of time.
5.	A special form for Reporting of Defects has been in use for quite some time. All road service personnel are instructed in its use and disposition. It is a requirement that all noticeable defects be reported to ensure repairs at terminals or, if possible, enroute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
That this House deplores the government's insensitivity and lack of action with respect to the critical problem of pollutants; in particular, that of mercury poisoning, which has had a destructive effect on the economic, social and health status of native people.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in a very personal way, I do not recall an issue that has concerned me more than that of the problem of mercury and its many ramifications. This motion before the House is in response to the government's insensitivity to the mercury problem and its obvious pretence that a social, economic and health crisis is non-existent. The problem has been particularly devastating to the native community. In human terms, it has been a tragedy of appalling proportions, and in the eyes of Canadians and the international community it has been a national disgrace.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who extols the virtues of the government's role in the development of a health care system, has viewed the problem with minimal interest and action. The minister was content to relegate the matter to an interdepartmental committee which is well recognized as the sophisticated bureaucratic method that is utilized to diffuse a non-priority item. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), who has a very special responsibility and mandate on behalf of native people and who should have provided strong, decisive leadership from the outset, has conveniently played the game of jurisdictional authority, again at the expense of native people.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand) has never viewed the problem in a serious manner and, indeed, a former minister of the environment, when addressing the executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association at the Royal York Hotel on April 8, 1970, clearly indicated that a problem did not exist. I quote as follows from his text entitled "The Polluter Must Pay":
Fortunately, we have caught our mercury problem in time. We have caught it before there has been any real danger to human beings. Once spotted, we have closed the fishery. Either that or we have bought up all the fish and had them destroyed. Nothing has escaped the watchfull eye of our federal inspection service, a service which is regarded the world over as tops.
I want to emphasize that the problem bridges provincial boundaries, that the problem today has grown in scope and magnitude and has ramifications, in my view, that demand a very strong federal presence. I want to make it emphatically clear that the major responsibility rests with federal authorities. Indeed, as the debate unfolds today I have no doubt the federal government can, and should, be censored for its role, or, more appropriately, its lack of role in this sordid affair.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Historically, the federal government has had a callous attitude in dealing with health problems affecting the native people-which constitutionally, I must remind the House, is a federal responsibility. Farley Mowat, in his book "The Desperate People" describes the virtual extinction of the inland Eskimos of the Keewatin district in the Northwest Territories. His chronicle of events should have served as an irrefutable argument for the necessity of immediate government intervention when the mercury problem first appeared. Father Rene Fumo-leau, a priest with years of service in the north, in his recent book "As Long as the Land Shall Last", in describing the 'flu epidemic of 1928 relates the unbelievable medical tragedies suffered by the aboriginal people of that day
May 7, 1976

and the failure of the federal government to respond to a crisis situation that affected human lives.
For a moment I would like to reflect on that tragic period in Canadian history as related by Father Fumoleau, because it is analogous to the problem we are debating today. If we substitute the word "mercury" for more familiar medical terms such as "tuberculosis," "smallpox", "measles" or "Spanish 'flu" which afflicted the natives of that day, one will find an amazing similarity not only in terms of human tragedy but in terms of government inaction.
Dr. Bourget, during his visits at that time to the territories in 1928, described a race attempting to survive but slowly dying from the white man's sickness. Influenza killed at least 200 in his area along the Mackenzie River in three weeks. Dr. Bourget predicted at that time that tuberculosis would become more active as a result of the Indian's weakened physical condition, yet despite pleas to Ottawa for medical help at that time his advice was ignored-and, of course, his predictions became reality.
In the years following the epidemic, Ottawa, despite the warning, actually reduced funds for the medical care of Indians. Between 1931 and 1934 the total budget for health services for all Indians in Canada dropped from $1,050,000 to $793,000, which included salaries for doctors, nurses, and transportation. By 1936 the government was paying less than $12 per year per Indian in the Northwest Territories for all medical services-and this was for a native population riddled with acute and chronic illnesses. Government directives during that period bordered on the inhuman and can best be characterized as lack of response to a problem which was felt by those in authority in Ottawa to be either exaggerated or of no importance.
The director of Indian Affairs advised all agents on January 14, 1934, that the department would expect a reduction in drug expenditures and demands of about 50 per cent. His directive went on to say that there would be no funds for tuberculosis surveys, treatment in sanatoria or hospitals, of chronic tuberculosis or other chronic conditions, nor in fact for any treatment except for acute sickness. In 1939 the department issued the following directive to Indian agents across Canada: a reduction of one day in the average length of stay of sick Indians in hospital would save about $15,000; it should not be difficult to save $10,000 in drug costs by limiting the amount of cough medicine, linaments, tablets, and so on, given to Indians. That black period in our history has reappeared in a new form, namely, mercury poisoning.
I have no doubt Canadians are shocked by these events and would consider the circumstances unconscionable in our society, yet it is precisely such an issue that is before us. As I stated previously, we have a social, economic and health crisis similar to the previous examples; but because new terminology-namely, mercury poisoning or Minamata disease-has been introduced, the government has attempted to mesmerize the public into believing the problem will magically disappear, and consequently has abrogated its responsibility to deal with the issue in a decisive and responsible manner.
Mercury Poisoning
I have been astonished by those in government who use the feeble excuse that mercury poisoning is an exotic disease recently discovered. Let me briefly place the matter in perspective. The mercury-contaminated fish problem came to the attention of the world in the city of Minamata, Japan, in 1953. Hundreds have died from that experience and thousands remain crippled, with an uncertain future. The problem has been well documented in the United States, Iraq and Sweden, again with scores of deaths and permanent neurological disability.
In 1964, at a major international conference, Dr. John Sprague, representing Canada from the Fisheries Research Board, was informed of the seriousness of the mercury problem by Dr. Jun Ui, and despite Dr. Sprague's interest and concern on returning to Canada no action was taken. In 1969, Jensen and Jernlov published the first report of aquatic organisms converting mercury to the far more toxic methyl mercury. Dr. Leo Buffa represented Canada at the International Mercury Conference at Prague in 1973 to obtain information for chloralkali regulations. At the international conference in Stockholm in 1970, Minamata patients were present with appropriate medical documentation. Surely the federal government was aware of these developments, and with the knowledge of industrial complexes in Canada utilizing mercury it could have taken active measures during this period to assess the magnitude of the problem.
Let me briefly refer to the Canadian situation. A brief prepared by the University of Saskatchewan and presented to the federal Department of Fisheries and Forestry in May, 1969, pointed out abnormal levels of mercury in fish taken from the Saskatchewan River below Saskatoon. Four months later, high mercury levels were found in fish taken from the Wabigoon River in northern Ontario. The discovery spread to the English River, and consequently the Wabigoon and English River systems were closed to commercial fishing in 1970. Mercury levels in fish from Clay Lake, northwest of Dryden, had the highest readings anywhere in the world, including fish obtained from the Minamata area. The Manitoba government lost its court case in the Supreme Court of Canada against mercury polluting companies upstream of Lake Winnipeg. Other parts of Ontario, including Lake St. Clair, the Detroit and St. Clair Rivers and the Ottawa River, have been affected. The Bell River system in Quebec is seriously polluted.
Following the ban on commercial fishing in Ontario forgivable loans were received by the affected fishermen. Despite the inadequacy of these loans, can the government possibly explain why the commercial fishermen at Mataga-mi have not received one cent in compensation? Can the government possibly explain why Dow Chemical was forced to change its process for handling effluents during 1970, yet the same action was not taken with Dryden and Domtar. The FMC plant in Squamish, British Columbia, has displayed effluent technology effective since 1971. One can only ask why this knowledge was not utilized by the federal government in establishing their chloralkali regulations.
Mr. Speaker, there are other examples. Surely the evidence is overwhelming that the federal government has had knowledge of a serious mercury problem for several years, but despite this fact it has displayed blatant disre-

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
gard for the seriousness of the problem, and only recently-and, I might add, under intense pressure-has it indicated some concern.
What has mercury pollution meant in human terms? The results have been devastating. We have seen self-sufficient native communities disintegrate. We have seen native people demoralized, and social chaos rise from the ashes while politicians and officials appear determined to pretend that no problem exists. Alcoholism, drunkenness, violence, crime and poverty have replaced self-sufficiency. Confrontation between the native and non-native population has replaced the need for a united front to fight a common enemy. The native, with his loss of traditional lifestyle, with his loss of independence and loss of dignity, has become the victim trapped in the jaws of an insensitive government.
As an example, among the principal benefactors of the fishing industry, both commercial and guiding, were two Indian reserves in the Dryden-Kenora area, namely, Grassy Narrows and White Dog. Others affected were shore workers in handling, processing, marketing, transportation and in supplying boats, gear, fuel and other commodities and services. What were the results? These two communities, which had previously been economically self-supporting, now are idle, dependent upon government handouts, and the people live in dread of the effect mercury will have on them and their children.
Before 1969 and the closure of the water system to commercial fishing, the total welfare budget for White Dog was substantially less than $50,000. By 1972 the figure was $93,550, and by 1974 it was $162,000. At Grassy Narrows the figure was less than $30,000 bere 1969, and had risen to $90,000 in 1971 and $122,000 by 1973. Prior to 1970, Ontario had 2,000 fishermen-56 in the Wabigoon, English and Winnipeg River systems. After the March, 1970, mercury fishing ban, approximately 240 Ontario fishermen were out of business, including all but three of the 56 in northwest Ontario. An estimated 250 natives from the two reserves were employed at tourist camps as guides, cooks and other jobs. Not only did they receive wages, but they frequently received gratuities and gifts to supplement their income. What has been the reward for these guides and tourist camp employees? Not one cent in compensation, but the risk of developing Minamata disease and the prospect of a number of guides recognized as high-risk patients having to return to guide work and continual eating of contaminated fish.
I do not for a moment underemphasize the impact the mercury problem has had on tourist camp owners, both those who have closed their doors in response to the health hazards and those who have remained open. Similarly, I do not under-emphasize the impact it has had on tourism in the area. All have suffered losses. However, the problem transcends the instinctive response of some individuals, fearful for their future, to use surreptitious methods, for reasons of self-interest, with risk to both native and nonnative people. The government's lack of response to these fears has, predictably, undermined the seriousness of the mercury problem, and by procrastinating it has not only compounded the fears of those affected but has delayed a positive response to the overriding issue of a serious environmental health problem.

On Tuesday, April 13, Bob Kabestra appeared before the Standing Committee on the Environment. His testimony was not one of anger or vengeance: it reflected the wisdom of his years, yet a sense of hopelessness for the future. Bob Kabestra had been a successful commercial fisherman, independent, self-sufficient and proud of his accomplishments. When his commercial fishing business was suspended he was making a good income: he owned three homes, three trucks, three boats with motors, nets and other equipment essential for his vocation. With the stroke of a pen, all his dreams and accomplishments were erased. Does the government have a conscience in response to his fate? Have they taken any action which would indicate he is a human being with a serious problem? Bob Kabestra does not think so, and I agree.
I should like to say a few words about Minamata disease, or mercury poisoning. I find it inconceivable that there should remain people who believe the disease entity is a myth and does not exist. Excluding the documented deaths and cases in other countries, I have stated in the past, and will repeat, that Minamata disease is a reality in Canada and I anticipate additional cases will be documented in the future. Dr. Andre Barbeau, director of the neurology department of the Montreal Institute of Clinical Research, well known for his discovery of L Dopa used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease, and who has worked with Japanese specialists in studying Minamata disease, has clearly demonstrated its presence in Cree Indians in Quebec and has also described symptoms in two white people.
From testimony we received at the standing committee on April 13, which has been confirmed by numerous articles, he has identified six definite cases, ten probable and several others tested as possible. Time does not permit a detailed analysis of the medical implications. Suffice it to say that there is overwhelming evidence related to such matters as length of time before symptoms appear, the added risk of continued exposure to those with known, elevated levels of mercury, the problems related to pregnancy, genetic and congenital problems, to indicate with a high degree of predictability that additional cases will appear. In addition, I am most concerned that a request which was placed before the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the president of Treaty No. 3, Fred Kelly, asking for assistance and for Dr. Barbeau to appear in that area as a known expert in neurology has received no response as yet from the Department of National Health and Welfare. Perhaps we will have some response in that respect today.
Notwithstanding the fact that there are individuals in government who are deeply concerned about the problems related to mercury-and I believe this view is shared by individual members in all corners of this House-I must re-emphasize that the government has not provided leadership to resolve, or indeed to formulate an effective program to deal with mercury and its many ramifications. Indeed, the government's record of inactivity is not only inexplicable but it is inexcusable. I have no doubt that government speakers will make reference to the recent rash of activity that has occurred within various departments on an ad hoc basis, but as Fred Kelly, president of Treaty No.
May 7, 1976

3, so aptly described the situation at the standing committee meeting on April 13, 1976, activity can only be measured in terms of effectiveness.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
If effectiveness is the appropriate criterion, and I readily accept that definition, then the federal government has failed dismally by not putting forward proposals in this respect. With the knowledge of a critical mercury problem in the hands of the government for several years, who on the government side is prepared or is able to defend the long period of inaction? There is no defence; there is only rationalization.
Why did the federal government refuse to invoke the federal Fisheries Act in the early 1970s before the chloralk-ali regulations were introduced? It was apparent the polluted waters crossed provincial boundaries, and if the act had been invoked and the Dryden plant had been closed for one day it would have alerted the native people, and indeed the surrounding communities, to the various procedures that would have been available to them in the courts.
We have evidence of a federal interministerial committee with NIB participation and provincial observers who had a mandate to collect and co-ordinate information concerning mercury. Prior to 1975 the meetings were infrequent, and despite numerous recommendations it was apparent their mandate was too restrictive; they had no decision-making capability and no secretariat to handle the workload. Again, no satisfactory explanation was given as to the lack of local native participation, and the lack of decision-making authority has made the body ineffectual.
The federal government was aware of the FMC plant in Squamish, B.C., that has had the technology since 1971 to keep their mercury discharge below the provincial and federal regulations, yet the regulations introduced are not based on this known FMC available and practical technology. There is no apparent effort to correlate the various scientific studies and to co-ordinate a plan effectively to overcome the adverse effects of pollution. In this regard it should be noted that on examination of mercury effluent reports from major chloralkali industries in Canada it was found there have been monthly averages during which the mercury discharge was above the standards set by regulation. Again, no explanation or action.
It is my understanding that the government is presently considering funding a litigation study, and hopefully we will have a response from the government in this regard before the debate is concluded. There is no effective way to place a monetary value on the destruction of a traditional way of life, yet compensation must be considered a priority item. The federal government has seen fit to assist in similar situations, for example, in James Bay. Is it any wonder the native communities have lost faith in the government? They have ignored native requests, native involvement and have simply responded with ad hoc, makeshift programs.
Testimony revealed that as recently as September, 1975, a native proposal for $60,000 to $70,000 to have mercury workers assist with the problems in the native communities was rejected by the Department of National Health and Welfare because they refused to recognize the presence of a mercury crisis. I have not heard serious objec-
Mercury Poisoning
tions raised to the $2.5 million directed to the Dryden Pulp and Paper Company from the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion, of which approximately $600,000 was spent in converting to a mercury-free process. However, when the transaction occurs under the umbrella of a public relations program, without regard to social, economic and health problems in the native communities, is it any wonder that cynicism and loss of confidence in the government prevails?
The critical problem of an alternate protein source of food has existed and continues to exist. I sense the importance of this matter has struck a respondent chord with government. But, again, the evidence is not convincing that the problem has been resolved. Let me also point out the obvious difficulties of convincing the native people in the communities affected to discontinue eating a longstanding stable of their diet when non-natives continue to eat fish from contaminated waters. In this regard I should also point out that there are studies to indicate abnormally high mercury levels may appear in these same individuals who consume contaminated fish for short periods, I ask the government, is this practice safe for the uninformed transient, and can the government assure these people that they will not be affected by this health hazard?
I ask the government, which undoubtedly has the authority, why they have refused to ban fishing in critical areas where cases of mercury poisoning have been clearly established. What are the government's plans to feed the natives at Matagami and Mistassini, Quebec, whose diet in the past consisted of 250,000 pounds of fish annually? Can this be replaced by other game? What other alternatives does the government propose? Will the government give favourable consideration to the excellent in-depth brief presented by the grand council of the Cree which includes the screening program for mercury in fish during 1976 at the Mistassini, Waswanipi and Niemiscau regions of James Bay?
This debate would not be complete without a comment about the Environmental Contaminants Act. I recall that when this legislation was introduced it was described as the most progressive piece of environmental legislation in any nation, and as the panacea to cure all environmental health problems. I viewed with skepticism the effectiveness of the bill, and I recall vividly the wide ministerial discretion which was embodied in it. One would be hard pressed to find an act in which the word "may" was used more frequently than in the Environmental Contaminants Act. The basic philosophy of the act can best be described as closing the barn door after the horse is out. The act has not been effective in this instance, and I respectfully submit that it requires significant amendments if it is, in fact, to be an effective piece of legislation to prevent environmental health hazards.
Out of this morass of callousness, insensitivity and pretence I think the question can logically be asked: Is there a solution? I believe the answer to that is an unqualified "Yes". Above all, the government must demonstrate a positive attitude, not only by words but also by action. It must demonstrate, in unequivocal terms, the necessity for a strong federal presence to deal with the basic issue of a

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
major environmental problem which affects both Indians and non-Indians alike.
For the immediate problem related to the communities directly affected by mercury pollution there is an obvious need for a central co-ordinating committee with a mandate for action and with meaningful input by those affected-in particular, native organizations. The natives have lost confidence in government and a legion of workers at this stage, irrespective of their good intentions, would be viewed with distrust and in my opinion would prove to be ineffectual. Confidence can only be regained at this late date by meaningful involvement of the communities affected and assurance of direct contact with the decision-makers.
When native reports have been rejected, when longstanding questions remain unanswered, when inconsistencies in the law exist, when endless delays for action are common, and when nameless faces revolve through desolate communities without solutions, is it any wonder the natives view with skepticism the sincerity of the government? Re-growth, the re-establishment of self-sufficiency, independence and a sense of dignity can only emanate from meaningful community involvement. I believe the Indian people have shown they are reasonable, capable and responsible in their approach to the problem, and their involvement should be a major priority.
There is an obvious need for a mechansim to serve as an early warning system for future environmental health problems so that decision-makers will have immediate information available to them. As I indicated previously, there is an obvious need for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to provide funds for legal aid. In this regard, the Minister of the Environment, in the same address to which I made reference at the outset, stated later in his speech to the executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association:
Our Freshwater Fish Marketing Board has already spent more than $300,000 helping to contain the mercury problem on the prairies.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will try to be brief in summarizing the remainder of my comments. I was quoting the Minister of the Environment, who said:
There, the local fishermen have been prevented from starving during the winter months. But the Canadian taxpayer cannot be expected to foot this bill for ever. Naturally, we are looking around for someone else to take the government off the hook. I suggest this someone else is the polluter. He must pay the bill in respect to mercury pollution, just as the Electric Reduction Company Limited footed the bill in respect to elemental phosphorous in Newfoundland in 1969.
Perhaps before termination of the debate the government will express in clear terms its present policy in this respect. There is need for a comprehensive review of the appearance of mercury in the Canadian environment, and surely this must be orchestrated by the federal government. Notwithstanding the fact that we have a mercury problem of crisis dimensions, with many known factors,

there continue to be many unanswered questions related to mercury which require comprehensive research and, again, surely this is a role for the federal government. The necessity for such research becomes more readily apparent when government members attempt to defend the indefensible by exploiting gaps in our knowledge, for political advantage, rather than admitting the obvious: that a problem exists. This approach is about as logical as rejecting cancer as a disease entity because we cannot effect a cure in all instances and because large gaps in knowledge persist which will only be bridged through research.
I have referred to the federal Fisheries Act and to the Environmental Contaminants Act. Suffice it to say that the former has not been invoked at times when it would have been constructive, and the latter requires amendments if it is to accomplish the goals for which it was introduced.
As I indicated by examples at the outset, and more specifically by the mercury problem, the entire attitude of the federal government toward the health of our native people is deplorable and is tantamount to negligence. I know the' Minister of National Health and Welfare is aware of the health status of native people, yet minimal corrective action is taken. Finally, I must emphasize that the mercury problem does not exist in isolation but is a prototype for innumerable environmental health hazards, many of which are directly related to occupations, but an equally large number are of potential risk to unwary Canadians. However, this is another topic. I have discussed this problem in the House on previous occasions, and simply reiterate at this time that there is clearly a role for the federal government to assume responsibility for the co-ordination of an effective program for environmental health problems which are clearly distinguishable from the traditional health problems identified with our health care system, which has been a provincial responsibility.
From the point of view of long-term planning, I was particularly disappointed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare rejected the fifth recommendation in the interim report entitled "Exposure to methyl mercury in Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves". Dr. T. W. Clarkson, professor and director for the centre for environmental health sciences of the medical school of the University of Rochester, called for the establishment of a national centre in environmental health to deal with environmental health hazards from methyl mercury and other pollutants. I spoke of a similar concept in this House on February 26, 1973, utilizing the national problem of drug and alcohol abuse as an example, and I suspect that this reasonable and responsible recommendation by Dr. Clarkson will receive the same attention and will gather the same dust!
I should like to conclude with one quotation from a favourite book of mine. Incidentally, the author was a physician. It is from "The Story of San Michele", by Axel Munthe, which I recommend to all hon. members. In a special preface for the American edition, he wrote:
The greatest writer of short sensational stories I know is life. But is life always true?
Mr. Speaker, I will await the government's response to his observation and his question.
