subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks on the important topic before the House, may I congratulate the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) for the excellent speech he made before lunch.
Some of the aspects of mercury poisoning relate to the poisoning of fish in the lakes, rivers and streams of this country. I have had some experience in looking after fish- believe it or not. In my office I have a couple of goldfish in a bowl. Every day I clean out the bowl and put in fresh water and food. Every day the fish eat the food, use its energy and put the waste product back into the water. There is no filter or pump in the bowl, and you can imagine how the bowl looks at the end of the day. It is so cloudy you can hardly see the fish. But that is all right for the fish, because it is my responsibility to come in the next day and flush out the bowl.
I think hon. members have been talking about the same sort of problem which troubles my fish. The difference is that no one seems willing to take the responsibility of flushing out our much larger fish bowl. There is another difference, Mr. Speaker. In our case the fish who make the water dirty are not the same fish that have to live in the water.
Hon. members will, I am sure, talk a great deal about mercury pollution and the poisoning of fish by mercury. Human beings consume these poisoned fish. But that is not our only concern. Most of us know that mercury-poisoned fish are eaten by bears, seals, otters, wolverines and other forms of wildlife on which our native people depend for their living. Really, what we are talking about is not new in Canada and is not restricted to Ontario and Quebec. For a number of years we have known about the presence of mercury and other industrial pollutants right across the country. We have known about this, but today we still quarrel over jurisdiction and liability. If we are to let the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) lead the way, we shall probably end up quarrelling over freezers.
Let us look at part of the record. In the Maritimes, as far back as 1971 officials in Nova Scotia were setting up task forces and other government agencies to examine how mercury was affecting the swordfishing industry. That was five years ago. We have just heard about conditions in Quebec, the province in which a company was allowed to dump mercury in quantities greater than the government's new regulations allowed to be dumped. They did this for a whole year after those regulations went into effect. Four of the people who show symptoms of Minamata disease live downriver from that plant.
I have heard some researchers claim that if and when the government releases enough money to do a thorough study
Mercury Poisoning
of northwestern Quebec, we shall find that all that region is contaminated by mercury. If we move to Ontario, we can isolate three separate areas which are contaminated by mercury. The northeastern part of the province is contaminated, including Lake Timiskaming. The water from that lake drains into the water of the Ottawa River which flows just behind your chair, Mr. Speaker. Still in Ontario, there is the English-Wabagoon River system. Mercury from these waters has caused symptoms of Minamata disease, as other hon. members have already pointed out. What is more, we have known about mercury contamination in the area for over five years. Then there is the St. Clair river, the first place, I think, to feel the effects of mercury pollution. We have known about that, too, for over five years.
I now come to Manitoba. That province is polluted by the same source of pollution which affected northwestern Ontario. We have know about mercury in Lake Winnipeg since at least 1970. Manitoba can also boast-if that is the appropriate term-of mercury pollution in two other river systems, the Saskatchewan and the Red rivers. We knew about pollution in those rivers as far back as 1970. Of course, Saskatchewan is represented on our list by the Saskatchewan River.
Then there is Alberta. If you read Time magazine of September 26, 1969, you will find a little story about mercury contamination in that province. It seems that mercury-based fungicides used on seed grain was the source of that contamination. It caused 100 per cent of the upland game birds tested in the southern part of the province to have mercury levels in their blood between 5 and 16 times greater than the maximum acceptable level. We knew about that in 1969, Mr. Speaker.
Then there are a couple of candidates for our list from what they call God's country-British Columbia. Back in April, 1970, the government had to close Upper Howe Sound to all fishing because of mercury contamination from a chemical plant in Squamish. Just to prove I am not being prejudiced, when I make this little list, I will throw in some examples from my own constituency. We seem to specialize in arsenic in Yellowknife. In 1969 researchers knew about it and did not tell anyone. We have mercury, too. In Yellowknife, in 1975, researchers from the National Indian Brotherhood found two little children who had excessively high levels of mercury in their hair. We also have fish with some of the highest readings in North America around Great Bear Lake and Tuktoyaktuk.
That is only a partial list, but it comes from right across the country. Right across the country we have documented cases of mercury contamination going back five and six years. We know what happened in Minamata, and we know that it takes over 100 years for a river system to flush itself of this pollutant. If we knew all these things, why in the name of all that is holy did we wait until 1976- when we have documented cases of congenital Minamata disease-to have a debate in this House? What has the government done in all the years that it has possessed this knowledge? Nothing, Mr. Speaker-nothing but the bare minimum to protect itself from obvious charges.

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
I would like to recommend that hon. members opposite pay a visit to some of the native communities affected by this pollution, or at least to look at pictures of victims in Japan. Then they would get an idea of what this disease does and how painful, crippling and long-lasting the symptoms are. Then there is the most unjust thing of all about this pollution, the victims. Who are they? It is not the plant owners who must live with the fact that their children will never be able to speak to them. It is not the members of Canada's "go-go" consumer society who will have their livehood taken away. They will not be forced to live the soul-destroying life of welfare hand-outs. It is not the people who produce the chemicals, or who consume them. The people who must bear this pain, this incredible cost, are native people. It disgusts me.
These are people who have learned to live with the land; who treat it as the source of their life and their culture; who respect the land. They are the ones who are being forced to pay this price. They are paying it so someone else can sell newsprint cheaply in New York, so someone else can benefit from the sale of our mineral wealth abroad. That is what this kind of pollution is, Mr. Speaker. It is a kind of tax, a kind of hidden cost of operation. We are living high and paying very little for it right now-at least most of us. The people who are picking up our tab for the free and irresponsible ride we are taking are native people. They choose to live a life close to the land, and when we destroy that land we destroy them. I cannot think of a slower, more agonizing way to destroy a person than Minamata disease.
Members opposite have chosen from their ranks an insurance salesman to look after the affairs of Indians. They tell me that insurance salesman are pretty good at figuring odds, longshots and that kind of thing. Well, if his department knew about the possible damage that mercury could do five years ago, they sure played a longshot. They gambled that if they did nothing, nothing would happen. They were wrong. They did nothing, and we now have children who are being born with Minamata disease. This happen because the honourable insurance salesman opposite does not understand the land. He and all the others like him are too busy developing frontier resources to worry about the mess they left behind in the last place they visited.
What they do is bash away to capitalize on undeveloped natural resources with adequate or untested technology. That is the cause of this problem. If the silver mine owners in northern Ontario had known in 1910 what they were doing with all the mercury they were dumping into the lake, if a responsible government had known the reaction, then we would not be in this situation now. However, they did not know, we are in this situation, and we still have not learned. We still have not learned because the expert on the longshots over there is still "gung-ho" on using untested and inadequate technology in the north. He is gambling that the same thing that happened with early chloralkali plants and silver extraction methods will not happen with the new technology in the north. He just does not understand what land means to native people. Look at the half-hearted solutions he has come up with. In Quebec, he and the people like him are going to make up for the lost protein by shipping in freezers. They ship in these freezers and then expect that extra moose and beaver caught during the hunting season will replace the fish. Well, by 
my rough calculation this method will wipe out the entire moose and beaver population in a very short time. That is what I call long, range planning! In Grassy Narrows the plan is to go with the freezer trick and add a lot of welfare. Eventually they are going to relocate the people. This is typical of the mentality displayed opposite: if you dirty up the fishbowl, so what, just move on. We native people know that you cannot just move on, and people like the insurance salesman over there will have to learn it soon. When they have finished leaving their mark on the Arctic, there will literally be no place left to move. They will have to start living in the sediment of their own fishbowl.
There has been a lot of buck-passing on this issue between the provincial and federal authorities. The responsibility clearly lies across the aisle here. The problem crosses provincial boundaries; it is a federal matter. The problem involves disruption of whole economies, and that is a federal matter. The problem involves native people; that is a federal matter, too. We have had five years of governments closing down fisheries, sending in freezers and grand welfare schemes. Why did we not see money, large amounts of money, committed to research into a means of stopping the destruction caused by mercury in the nervous system? Why did we not have pollution inventories in all areas where the possibility of mercury and other heavy metal pollution exists? We knew about it over five years ago. If we had done it then, maybe one or two of the people who now have Minamata disease would be healthy today.
Why, in 1972, when the new regulations for mercury came into effect, was there any mercury allowed at all? Everyone knew at that time that the chloralkali process was becoming outdated. Everyone knew that as soon as the present equipment had been written off it would be replaced by a process that did not use mercury. Why did the government not ban it entirely then? It would have cost the pulp and paper industry a lot of money, for one thing. They would have had to replace all that equipment early. But what has it cost the Cree of Mistassini? What price do you put on a child with congenital Minamata disease?
For 400 years native people have tried to help the European adapt to this land. It was easy at first. He needed our food and our ways to survive. However, we were unable to teach them one thing: you cannot destroy the land because the land sustains you. Now that we are one step away from filling this continent completely, I hoped that this lesson would have been learned. Apparently it has not. Look at it this way. We have tried to maintain our culture, based close to the land, for 400 years. It has not been easy. We have paid. Goodness knows we have paid. We have been forced to share our land with a culture that tried to assimilate us-tried to make us like them. Well, it did not work- at least until they invented this new tactic of destroying the very basis of our lives. It does no good to give us fish from other lakes. It does no good to give us welfare and take away our self-respect, and no good to move us to another place. These things do no good because we know that you cannot move away from your own fishbowl once you destroy it.
The government should finally start to act, to assess the damages where they belong, that is, on the companies that
May 7, 1976

did the polluting in the first place, and from the public purse because the public allowed it to happen. We should have massive funding to work with the Japanese to find ways of containing mercury in both the environment and in the human nervous system. We need the development of alternate economies where our own have been destroyed, economies that will give native people their livelihood without the extremely high cost of welfare.
For a long time the government has allowed criminal negligence to occur and, Mr. Speaker, we do not need any more freezers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today focuses on the critical problem of pollutants and in particular on mercury poisoning. I should like to deal primarily with the technical aspect of this problem and try to illustrate the perspective of the problem with respect to time-relating what has been going on, why it has and is taking the time it has and is taking, and what results there are and can be expected.
This is an area which primarily relates to research and development. One of the big problems that I have found in parliament in Ottawa is that most people do not know what research and development is, how it works and how long it takes. Research and development is not like a water tap that you can turn on and off. You can turn if off all right, but it will take seven years to turn it on again and get results. That is a good example of the time it takes to get results when tackling a serious problem such as this one and all the problems of pollution that face us in this generation.
There are several problems of pollution which are extremely important-asbestos, with the problem of asbe-stosis and radiation, especially natural radiation where you have radium which decomposes into radon, and radioactive gas. Government and industry have tackled this problem. In the mining of uranium ore, Eldorado Mines has installed extensive ventilation equipment to remove the radon gas in order to prevent miners being exposed to it. There are lead and arsenic and the problems of pollution and poisoning that have resulted from their use and abuse. We have learned more about them and how to eliminate the problem. On the question of organic phosphates, it is not too many years since Shell was bragging about TCP- tri-cresyl phosphate-in gasoline. Now, a decade later, we realize that this is a serious chemical pollutant which causes serious toxic problems which have to be dealt with. We are now trying to come to grips with the problems of organic phosphates.
The Great Lakes is another classic example of a problem that took years and years to develop before it was finally recognized and action was taken. Even though a tremendous amount of work is being done on the problem, it will take many years to clean up the Great Lakes, the worst one being, of course, Lake Erie. Although a lot of work has been done over the last decade, a great deal more still has to be done. The signs are, however, that we are beginning to win this terrible battle on pollution.
The motion before the House primarily deals with mercury and I will concentrate most of my remarks on that problem. It is only one of a vast array of pollutants, however, that we have to deal with. To illustrate how
Mercury Poisoning
seriously the federal government considers this problem, I would point out that the federal Department of the Environment is the largest technical department of the federal government. There are many times when I wish other departments had more money to spend on technology and people to do research and development. This is an important area of the environment, however, and the federal government takes it seriously.
Is mercury a new problem? Is it a new material? Far from it, Mr. Speaker. You will recall that the manufacture of hats involves mercury. You will have heard the term "as mad as a hatter", or you may remember that in "Alice in Wonderland" there was a character called the Mad Hatter. The madness was due to mercury poisoning. When mercury is ingested it goes to the brain, the liver and the kidneys. It has deleterious effects on the brain that result in madness. Mad hatters have been known for a long time. Government and industry finally realized the danger and took steps to eradicate it. In 1947, as a result of the joint effort of government and industry, the mercury process for the treatment of rabbit fur in the making of hats was discontinued and an acid-carotin process was used to treat fur for the manufacture of hats. Mercury is no longer used in the hat industry and we do not have that pollution problem.
There are several sources of mercury, Mr. Speaker. The natural sources are the degassing of the earth's surface, evaporation by wind action, and volcanic action falling again on the earth's surface as rain. These sources contribute up to 50,000 tons per year-no small amount, Mr. Speaker. The contribution from manufacturing processes is about 10,000 tons per year, or one-fifth of what occurs naturally, both organic and inorganic. These come from various sources such as the chloralkali process which contributes about 25 per cent, the electrical industry which contributes a further 20 per cent, the paint industry which is responsible for 15 per cent, control and measuring devices a further 10 per cent, and the balance from such uses as dentistry where you have mercury amalgam, and detonators which use mercury fulminate.
Mercury is also released in the combustion of fossil fuels. Mankind may liberate up to 20,000 tons of mercury per year in the environment both as organic and inorganic mercury. This may be localized in hot spots where you have combustion-near mines, smelters, chemical plants and other areas of large-scale combustion. Mercury contamination on this earth is not due only to manufacturing, commercial and industrial uses. What are the levels of mercury that we must be concerned about? No element on this earth exists in zero concentration. Sometimes the amount is very difficult to measure, but we should know the problems and the limits. In humans, mercury is measured both in the blood and in the hair. Twenty parts per billion is now regarded as the maximum acceptable level although 100 parts per billion was the previous level, now this is retained as the lower level of the "at risk" group.
Mercury turns up in fish. I will explain more about how that happens later. In uncontaminated water-water completely removed from any commercial source of mercury pollution anywhere in the world-fish are produced with a range of mercury of .03 to .2 parts per million. So with no mercury contamination from an industrial source there

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
will still be residual mercury in fish. There is no such thing as fish without any mercury content at all. The question is, what level is safe? The lower level recently suggested for fish when it forms a significant proportion of the diet, as with the Indian people, is .2 parts per million. The maximum level of tissue mercury acceptable in fish for commercial purposes is .5 parts per million. I will to refer to these levels later, but I wanted to put them on the record as a frame of reference.
The knowledge of how mercury gets into fish is very recent. In the fall of 1969, in Sweden, two scientists discovered that metal mercury in biologically active water such as that found in rivers very slowly converts into methyl mercury. Methyl mercury is a very toxic substance which is absorbed by many biological creatures, including fish.
It was in 1969 that for the first time it was realized that what had originally been thought of as inert material, metallic mercury, was able to change into a very toxic poison and get into the biological system. In the following spring of 1970, a few months later, action was taken by the provincial government of Ontario which launched a legal action against several companies in the chemical producing area near Sarnia, Ontario. The action was launched against Dow Chemical of Midland, Michigan, Dow Chemical of Canada in Sarnia, and against Wyandotte Chemicals of Michigan. Unfortunately, that legal battle is continuing to this day and is still not resolved. One of the reasons for this long delay is that a statement of claim had to be filed and was not filed until last year. The defence could not file their claim until a claim had been filed by the claimants.
Although the court case is not yet resolved, this did not stop the company from taking action, and it immediately took preventive measures to curtail the leakage of mercury from these mercury cells that were producing chlorine and caustic soda, or sodium hydroxide, in the Dow plant at Sarnia to the levels prescribed by the provincial government. They gathered as much information as they could, as quickly as possible, and came to appreciate the problem involved in trying to keep mercury down to a negligible level. They had to reduce it down to a teaspoonful a day, but still felt that was not satisfactory; so they ended up spending $40 million to replace this process by a diaphragm process whereby no mercury is used at all; the electrolyte mercury in this chlorine cell is changed to salt brine which is used instead. With no mercury in the process, there is consequently no mercury contamination or pollution.
It was the decision of the company to spend $40 million. This is no small expenditure, as I am sure hon. members will appreciate, and caused the company several problems in coming to this decision. This action was taken in 1970 and the new process, the diaphragm cell, was completed in 1973. In that year the mercury cells were closed down and the buildings torn down. So that Dow Chemical of Sarnia no longer has any chlorine cells in the mercury process, or any mercury pollution.
What was the result of that mercury going into the river system? Some of it very slowly, as we found out, became methyl mercury and was picked up by plant life in the

area, consumed by the fish life and was incorporated into the liver and brains of the fish. The people downstream from this are the Chippewas of Sarnia, some of them living on the reservation on Walpole Island. There are 1,400 people located in the Lake St. Clair area. Several samplings were taken during the early 1970s and these confirm that there was a problem there of mercury pollution. Blood samples have been taken for quite some time, as recently as November and December of 1975. Of these recent samples, which are part of an ongoing program, 162 results were obtained. Some 150 were under the 20 parts per billion level and only one was over the 50 parts per billion level, indicating a serious problem. So that 150 out of 162 results proved to be well below the level prescribed by the health officials. A health education program has been started and persons with levels over 20 parts per billion are being retested and will be retested every three months. A review of the dietary habits in this area indicates that there is little reliance on fish as the principal source of protein, and therefore a protein replacement program was not required, as it has been elsewhere in Canada. That gives the House a few details as to what one company has done, how it was done and how it fits into the total program.
The federal government, with provincial co-operation, has taken a number of steps over the past five years to deal with the health threat posed by high levels of mercury found in fish that are the staple diet of Indians living in boreal areas. In a joint statement last September, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the then Minister of the Environment, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development expressed the federal government's continuing grave concern regarding the health threat to Indians who continue to catch and eat fish known to be contaminated with mercury and outlined further measures being taken by the government to deal with the problem.
The ministers indicated that the federal government had taken steps to deal with mercury pollution problems in two areas, Dryden in northern Ontario and Quevillon in northwestern Quebec, and to head off similar situations elsewhere. Fish taken by the Grassy Narrows and White Dog . Indian bands from the Wabigoon-English River system are unsuitable for human consumption due to mercury contamination. The Dryden Chemical Company is known to have discharged significant quantities of inorganic mercury prior to the institution of effluent controls. Similarly fish consumed by the Cree Indians in the Waswanipi-Lac Quevillon area of northwestern Quebec have been contaminated by mercury from natural and industrial sources, including the Domtar complex. The health threat arose as a result of inorganic mercury being converted to toxic methyl mercury by bacteria in bottom sediments and entering the aquatic food chain and accumulating in fish tissue.
The ministers outlined a program that has been carried out with the co-operation of the provincial authorities in regard to health protection measures. Several measures are being taken and I should like to list them for the House. One has been a mercury control program which was instituted beginning in 1970. A second measure was inspection programs by the fisheries and marine service of the Department of the Environment to ensure the safety of all fish products marketed in Canada. A third measure

involved the departments concerned carrying out for several years a campaign for educating the Indians in the two areas about the true dangers of eating contaminated fish. These areas were closed to commercial fishing in 1970 and have remained closed since that time.
Fourthly, Mr. Speaker, a health team familiar with the mercury problem has been working in each of these areas. Fifthly, alternative food is being provided to the Grassy Narrows and White Dog bands through the co-operation of the provincial authorities and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. A similar program is being developed for those affected in northwestern Quebec.
Sixthly, the province of Ontario has identified lakes where Indians can fish safely for food, and community freezers are being provided to store these fish. The last measure undertaken concerns economic development opportunities, including the establishment of a canoe manufacturing facility and shoe factory, which are being pursued with the assistance of other federal departments.
The Department of National Health and Welfare began to monitor the levels of mercury in humans in northwestern Ontario and northwestern Quebec in 1971 when the levels of mercury in fish were found to be above the limits permissible for human consumption. Mercury levels in blood and hair samples were found to be elevated in persons with a dietary history of significant fish consumption from contaminated areas. As a result, an educational program was commenced in both areas warning people to stop eating the contaminated fish.
In addition, a group of Indians from northwestern Quebec who had blood levels in excess of 100 parts per billion of mercury was admitted to the Montreal Neurological Institute for a complete assessment. A similar group from northwestern Ontario was investigated in Winnipeg. In addition to routine hospital tests, detailed neurological examination as well as electromyelograms and nerve conduction studies, electroencephalograms, audiograms, visual field determinations and blood cytogenetic studies were carried out. No findings specifically attributable to methyl mercury excess were detected. The results of these tests were reported to the persons concerned and made public in summary form.
There is no known effective treatment for damage to the nervous system caused by mercury poisoning. Japanese experience indicates that mercury poisoning may develop from chronic exposure to mercury, even at relatively low blood mercury levels. For these reasons and because the mercury levels in fish caught in the areas concerned will remain unacceptably high for some years, even with controls on further pollution, National Health and Welfare has based its health protection efforts on warning the people not to eat contaminated fish, while monitoring their health status. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, with provincial co-operation, has arranged for the provision of fish from alternative sources in northwestern Ontario and is developing similar plans in northwestern Quebec.
On finding in 1974 and 1975 that blood levels of mercury in some individuals in both northern Ontario and north-
Mercury Poisoning
western Quebec were still in excess of 100 parts per billion, and even above 500 parts per billion in three people in northwestern Quebec, the education and monitoring program has been intensified. Dr. Tom Clarkson, an international authority on mercury toxicity, has been engaged by National Health and Welfare and has conducted an epidemiological assessment of the problem on the reserves in northwestern Ontario. An interim report was released in January of this year.
In addition, a fully equipped departmental mobile laboratory has been set up so that on-site blood and hair analysis can be carried out. Local practitioners are co-operating in the program. The Department of National Health and Welfare is sending in medical specialists, neurologists and opthalmologists to assist the health team on the reserves in screening for signs of mercury toxicity. A nutritionist is counselling the people on diet supplementation and compiling dietary histories.

speechtext:
I understand that priorities on the opposite side of the House are not in respect of public welfare and public well-being.
To continue, in northwestern Ontario, community people have been hired to intensify the educational program using local approaches in getting across the importance of not eating fish taken from contaminated areas. Working with community health representatives, health professionals and health educators, they have developed an audio-visual program and have commenced a household by household campaign. Similar programs are being developed in northwestern Quebec.
The government is looking for co-operation from the native associations and native leadership to assist in explaining the problem to the native people. The government has encouraged and supported the involvement of the native people in efforts to come to grips with the problem. Government support has included the provision of funding

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
for a visit by a native group from the Dryden area to Japan to see at first-hand situations in Japan where the established case of mercury poisoning in a fish-eating population has occurred.
A previous environment minister said that regulations controlling the discharge of mercury in chloralkali plant effluents were enacted in early 1972. The Dryden plant began operating in 1962; the Domtar plant at Quevillon in northwest Quebec has been operating since 1967. From the time the control requirements were initiated, mercury losses in chloralkali effluents have been reduced to 1 percent of pre-control levels. In general, levels of mercury in fish from the English-Wabigoon Rivers system have decreased from average levels of 4 parts per million to approximately 2 parts per million since mercury control regulations were instituted. The plant at Dryden was converted to the non-mercury process in November of last year.
Although direct discharges of mercury to receiving waters have been drastically reduced during the last three years, ministers are concerned with the large amounts of mercury discharged during past decades. Bottom sediments of some river systems are contaminated with mercury. That contamination undoubtedly continues to find its way through the aquatic food chain. Considerable effort is being devoted at this time to finding solutions to this problem. Fisheries and marine service scientists at the Freshwater Institute in Winnipeg are examining mercury in various levels of the ecosystem in the waters of northwest Ontario in order to determine the rate of disappearance of mercury from the environment.
During my tour of the fisheries laboratory in Halifax last month I was able to learn that mercury studies have been conducted there on harp seals in conjunction with the University of Guelph. They have been detecting and determining the effects of mercury on seals and the mercury poisoning of herds, since it is known that these seals have had a high content of mercury and have been eating fish contaminated with mercury. The program was completed after a year of study and the results have just been reported.
Studies also at Halifax are going on in the area of cod where their reproductive system is being investigated to see if this may not be one of the factors contributing to the depletion of fish stocks off the maritime coast. Other contaminants are also being looked at at the same time. In addition to mercury, this includes arsenic, cadmium, polychlorinated biphenyls and organic phosphates which I mentioned earlier. Ministers noted that the problem in northwest Quebec was more difficult to deal with because there are high natural levels of mercury in the waters of certain lakes and rivers. In addition, the Indian people of the Waswanipi area have a nomadic lifestyle that involves a broad area and with few fixed communities.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go on record as disagreeing with the mover of the motion who said that the government is inactive and has done nothing. I think I have shown by my comments that the government has been very concerned, very active and has an ongoing program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin today with a quotation from Solzhenitsyn, who said:
I used to think that experience of life can be handed on from one nation to another and from person to person. But now I am beginning to have my doubts about this. Perhaps everyone is fated to live through every experience himself in order to understand.
How true that rings today after the experience of Japan. The Minamata disease was so clearly evident, so clearly misunderstood and misinterpreted here in Canada. I think we should begin by looking at the problem briefly.
We have just heard a dissertation about the great things being done by the government of Canada. That speech flies in the face of the expert witnesses who appeared before the committee. They gave a more true and more accurate picture.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Who were those witnesses? I speak today neither as a chemist nor as a scientist of any kind. My references are not from politicians but are from the great academics of our nation and nations abroad.
I shall quote the expert testimony of Dr. Peter A. Larkin from British Columbia, and Dr. Louis Azzaria from Quebec. From Ontario I shall quote Dr. Clarkson. I shall also quote the environmentalist writer, Ms. Smith. Testimony was presented before the committee. At the committee it was stated that the World Health Organization safety level for mercury in fish has been set at .5 parts per million. Testimony showed that Canadian waters register at ten times that. The government even has conceded that the levels in some areas of Canada are 15 to 30 times greater that the safety level in respect of mercury pollution. One case at the White Dog reserve is described where the blood level of an infant at birth was 100 parts per billion. Other tests showed that it would take 100 years for the environment naturally to process the mercury currently there to a state that would reach the international standard set by the World Health Organization.
What do we see? We see that it will take 100 years just for the natural dissolution of the mercury in our environment. In answer to my question whether there is an overall increase or whether the increase is stabilized the expert witness said that it is certainly going up. So we are not
May 7, 1976

merely talking of the problem of today, but an increasing problem. He said:
If we compare the figures of the thirties with the figures for the seventies, there is a fourfold increase. So we are certainly going up. That is the direction we are going.
That is the specific and expert testimony. In addition to that and other testimony, I might quote from Dr. Peter Larkin, who said:
I think it might interest the committee to know, that there is, to my knowledge, no comprehensive review of the occurrence of mercury in the Canadian environment, and a review would be desirable.
Dr. Azzaria says:
The important issues are the people who have been affected by mercury poisoning-They have definite cases of mercury poisoning. This is where the priority lies.
Ms. Smith, co-author of "Minamata", says:
-both in Minamata and previous outbreaks in Japan-the effect was not noticed in the human population until several years after contamination had begun.
We heard other testimony from the government side to the effect that the blue fin tuna caught off the east coast of Canada is not allowed to be consumed in Canada, while we do export for consumption in Japan, of all places. We hear from Dr. Azzaria that some of the mercury has been transported aerially long distances from important industrial centres in North America. We heard, also, that there has been very little variation in the Greenland ice sheet between the year 800 B.C. and 1952. There had been very little variation in the increase in mercury contamination, while in the period 1962 to 1965 the concentration in that icefield doubled.
These are just some of the statements which show that the problem is not in hand. The solutions are neither known nor implemented. The fact that this is so is a condemnation of the government of Canada for its ineffective action in respect of this program. We have just heard a scientific-dissertation by a chemist. I want to say to the members of this House that this is not merely a matter of chemistry or a dissertation. Let us look at the problem that really exists. As I stated in respect of an earlier quotation, this is a problem in which somehow it seems that everyone is fated to live through every experience himself so to live. I hope no member on the opposite side of the House will ever have to live through Minamata disease.
I still feel they have an obligation to try to understand the feelings of the people suffering from this disease. In that respect, I shall send to the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) a book of pictures that will help him understand-because he is a member and parliamentary secretary-the feelings of the people who suffer from this disease. Let us look at some of the quotations. What does this disease do? How does it affect the human body? I shall quote again from the expert evidence of the witnesses. This is an indication of what Minamata does in relation to the human being who suffers from it. In extreme cases you can see a person having terrible convulsions, with twisted limbs, and collapsing. However, in most cases what happens is that there is a severe inability to co-ordinate. If you want to reach for a glass of water, you have to be able to think very hard to be able to move your fingers.
Mercury Poisoning
Then there is further testimony to this effect concerning what Minamata is like and how it reacts. Children are born completely crippled, with very severe mental retardation. They are often blind, with twisted limbs. They are unable to walk, unable to eat on their own, and so on. The children born after the occasion in Japan are now attending regular schools. It is found that there is a mental deficiency of 29 per cent, and much higher percentages of sensory disturbance and co-ordination problems. These are the real problems which exist and which we must learn to feel and understand. We learned that Lake Winnipeg, the St. Lawrence River, Lake Erie, Lake St. Clair, the Ottawa River, the Saskatchewan River system, and the Red Deer River were only a few of the major bodies of water in Canada polluted to a significant degree with mercury.
Worst of all is the English-Wabigoon system near Dryden in northwestern Ontario and northwestern Quebec. Residents in both these areas show dangerously high concentrations of mercury in their blood and hair, and some display the early symptoms of Minamata disease. Mercury poisoning, or Minamata disease, occurs when inorganic mercury, usually from chemical factories, is discharged into bodies of water and lodges in the bottom sediments. There it is converted by bacteria into toxic organic mercury, which works its way up the aquatic food chain to man. It then attacks the neurological system, leading to physical deformation, mental deterioration and eventually death.
In pregnant women, excessive levels of organic mercury can lead to abortion or to the birth of mentally retarded or congenitally deformed children. No one knows the true extent of mercury pollution in Canada. In the cases of mercury poisoning that we are aware of, the federal government has attempted to shift the responsibility to the provinces. As Mrs. Smith put it: "I have seen something that I would have to call extreme inaction." That is a description of the government's program that was described to us earlier today. What needs to be done? Dr. Larkin summed it up this way:
In particular, there are needs for research on how you might remove mercury from fish in processing them for human consumption, research on medicines that might increase the rate at which people might eliminate mercury that they had taken into their food. There is particular need for research on techniques of removing accumulations of mercury from bottom sediments in rivers and streams. There is need for search concerning safe levels of human consumption of different forms of mercury, the rates at which they are eliminated and the kinds of damage they do, including the effect on unborn infants.
I think it is important to realize that the research that is needed on mercury is of a very sophisticated nature. It is the sort of area in which I would think it was essential that there should be federal involvement . . .
I also think there should be federal funding. Certainly such research programs are cheap at half the price when you consider that in Japan corporations and government have paid out $83 million in claims to victims of this disease.
In addition to that, while we recognize the need for long-term research, as Ms. Smith also said, we need to recognize that now is the time for immediate action to ensure that people do not continue to consume contaminat-

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
ed fish, because there is evidence that this is occurring at present.
We also require an immediate and comprehensive review. At present there are such unrelated reviews with respect only to water, but we should move far beyond the surveillance and examination of water because we find that the basic sources of from 40 per cent to 65 per cent of mercury in the environment are unknown.
In addition to a comprehensive review we must examine the monitoring systems and we must police them better. We were told in the testimony before the committee that at present the monitoring systems are not standardized. The tests that are taken are ineffective, inaccurate, and deceptive because they are taken at times of the year when mercury levels are low and in areas where people are not eating a full diet of fish. So the monitoring program, as stated so ably by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), should be reviewed, and if time allows me I will go into that in detail in a few minutes.
Let us look at government action on these programs. It seems to me that the action of the government has resulted in inaction, or at least inadequate action. Let us look at what its supporters did in committee. When we sat in committee, what was the response of our counterparts on the Liberal side? There were attempts to discredit witnesses and attempts to block motions calling for further and full investigation into this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in this very important debate on the problem of mercury pollution in Canada, especially in northern Ontario, a region which I represent in my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie. The concern that many of us have on a nation-wide scale has been dramatized recently by the revelations of mercury

poisoning in the water systems of northwestern Ontario, especially in the White Dog and Grassy Narrows Indian reserves.
One does not have to dramatize mercury poisoning. Anyone who has witnessed even still photographs of what that does to the nervous system and how it creates deformity in human beings, and anyone who has seen films of victims of this kind of poisoning will know that it is a dreadful and shattering experience to see fellow human beings in fits of convulsion because of an industrial pollutant like this which has been allowed to go into our river systems, into fish, and hence into the human food chain.
This disease is not new. It has been thoroughly researched in Japan because there have been hundreds of victims of mercury poisoning there, and the native people of northwestern Ontario and elsewhere have been concerned about the pollutants which large industries have been pouring into the air and also into the water systems. Evidence of mercury poisoning has been building up in the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves for a number of years, and despite the evidence and the current revelations, especially the testimony on Minamata disease of expert Japanese scientists who have visited the native people, we see the companies responsible ignoring their responsibility and denying that they have anything to do with the pollution problem.
We see governments not taking action to clean up the pollution mess or to compensate the native people for the loss of their jobs and the destruction of their environment. We also see the general public which, except for a brief "tut, tut" when it sees a newsfilm or reads an article, lapsing back into complacency about this very severe problem which is destroying the livelihood and the health of a number of Canadians.
I weigh what I am going to say with careful concern and consideration, but I believe that had this been a white community at White Dog or Grassy Narrows, this mercury pollution problem would have been cleaned up years ago.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
We know that since 1960 mercury has been put into the Wabigoon and English River System by the Dryden Chemical Company, a subsidiary of Reed Paper Ltd. In May of 1970 the Ontario government announced that the mercury pollution problem was not serious in this area and that it would go away in a few months. We have heard expert testimony that it will take at least 100 years for the river system to cleanse itself of this dangerous pollutant.
In 1973 the Ontario Conservative government put up signs saying "Fish for Fun" for all the people who were fishing in that river system. The native people of these areas do not fish for fun, they fish for their livelihood, to feed themselves and their children, and that kind of callous action is little compensation or relief for people who depend on fishing for their well-being.
In March of 1975 the Ontario government sent letters to reserve residents telling them either to eat no fish, to eat less fish, small fish, or fish with lower mercury levels. Where is responsible government concern demonstrated in that kind of action and advice for the native people?
In 1975 Japanese scientists familiar with Minamata disease visited the Grassy Narrows reserve and began investigations to prepare a report to prod political leaders to take some action and clean up pollution, but what did the provincial minister of natural resources, Leo Bernier call them? He called them a travelling pack of troubadors. That is how the provincial government viewed respected scientists and their concern for the problems of the native people.
In April, 1975, evidence showed that the Dryden Chemical Company had been emitting seven and a half pounds of mercury per day into the river system, whereas the native people and the rest of Canada had been assured by the government that the amount was only a few ounces per day. We have, supposedly, effective anti-pollution legislation at both the federal and provincial levels to give governments power to regulate pollution in terms of discharge into the air or into the water system. If seven and a half pounds per day, which exceeds the maximum level, is being emitted, why is that allowed to go on? Again, the answers are not forthcoming. It is indicative of a callous indifference on the part of the provincial and federal governments.

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
The provincial government offered freezers to the people on the reserves to store non polluted fish or to encourage them to hunt for game and other food sources. As my colleague, the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) pointed out, that kind of policy would deplete the animal food supply in the area within a few short years.
In terms of human health I have pointed out that the disease is a terrible one for any human being to suffer. There has been research in Japan, Sweden, and Canada to try to bring about a solution to the problem. Despite the fact that so much research has gone on, the frightening thing is that much of it has not become public knowledge or implemented, and that the results of that research are not used to solve the problem. There was a five year test program on the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves. There was a joint Quebec-federal government mercury investigation in northwest Quebec. The report was presented in 1975. The federal Department of National Health and Welfare sponsored environmental research to study the blood and hair tissue of people living in areas which were thought to be contaminated. We have all these reports, but still no action.
The National Indian Brotherhood has conducted its own independent study. It has made recommendations, and still, except for more pious promises that further research will be done, there has not been effective action to control this dangerous pollution problem. The governments at both levels are aware of the problem but they deny their information to the native people. They have told the native people to be patient, that more research must be done, and that the problem is not as serious as they think. In the meantime we see more and more evidence of children, men, and women having symptoms of mercury poisoning or Minamata disease. It has affected the health of native people, their whole livelihood, their incomes, and their standard of living.
I now wish to put on record the story of Mr. Joe Payash, a 30-year-old man with seven children, who lives on Grassy Narrows Reserve, northwestern Ontario. In the story to which I am referring he explains the economics of the reserve. This man, Mr. Speaker, is taking welfare for the first time in his life. Last summer he was a guide at one of the fishing lodges. He will probably return next summer despite the dreadful knowledge that the traditional shore lunch of mercury-laden fish he must eat each day with the tourists who have hired him may some day kill him. He is paid $24 a day for guiding two people in a boat, and has done it all his life. Today he has stomach pains and a tightness across his chest, which may or may not be symptoms of mercury poisoning. He does not know. The last time his blood was tested he was told he had 210 parts per billion of mercury, a dangerously high level. The currently acceptable maximum level believed safe by the Ontario government is 100 parts per billion. As he says, "But it's the only way I can work, the only way I know how to earn a living."
It is not good enough to send freezers so that the native people may store non-contaminated fish. It is not good enough to say to them, "We need to do further studies." It is not good enough to say to them that we cannot enforce our environmental laws, and it is not good enough to tell

them we don't know if the Dryden chemical plant is the polluter. Those people face economic ruin while the government delays and does not bring forward adequate programs which can help to redesign the economy of those affected areas.
It is interesting to note that the native people of those reserves now live in a state of welfare because, through no fault of their own and because of lack of effective environmental laws in this country, an industry has polluted the river system from which they gained their livelihood. Before 1969 the total welfare budget on White Dog Reserve was below $50,000. By 1974 the budget had risen to $162,000. Similarly, on Grassy Narrows Reserve the total welfare budget in 1969 was about $30,000. By 1973 it had risen to $122,000.
We have heard stories of the social disintegration of families and neighbourhoods in the area, of people turning to drink in desperation, of alcoholism which is rampant and increasing, of increased violence involving assault and shooting, of husbands and wives separating and children suffering because homes are broken, all because the government has not accepted responsibility, or has not made private industry accept responsibility for destroying the livelihood of these people.
In the limited time available I will try to make positive suggestions as to a course of action the federal government can take. The federal government cannot pass the buck and say this is a provincial responsibility, because the English-Wabagoon river system crosses the provincial boundaries and therefore comes under federal jurisdiction. The federal government has the power, under environmental laws, to get tough, and it will if it seriously wants to do something about the problem. It can say to polluting companies, "Clean up." The federal government can introduce legislation which will make the companies compensate the victims of the pollution the companies have caused. It is not good enough to slough off the problem and say that the companies have not polluted. The problem is there. The companies have polluted. It is time they accepted their responsibilities.
The federal government can assist the companies to install better equipment which will prevent pollution of the environment. It can do this by passing laws and, if necessary, by giving tax incentives to speed the process. As well, we can adopt some of the suggestions made by the Japanese scientists who visited northwestern Ontario. Their recommendations, based on their expertise and experience, are well worth-while. They recommended as follows:
1.... Stop all consumption of the contaminated fish and make the natives aware of the seriousness of the situation.
2.	An intensive and indepth examination be performed on all the inhabitants of the area by competent and experienced physicians.
3.	That such a study be carried out under the auspices of Dr. Newberry, the reserve's resident physician, because he understands the situation and is knowledgeable about the Dryden-Kenora mercury pollution problem.
4.	That native people and other concerned citizens ask for comprehensive compensation to pay for the damage to the health and life style of the Dryden-Kenora residents.
5.	'Continue and promote the co-operation and exchange of experience with the victims in Japan, as well as with the supporting experts, domestic and foreign.'
May 7, 1976

6.	All data on mercury pollution be made public, especially to those concerned.
7.	Participation of natives in the decision making bodies dealing with White Dog-Grassy Narrows mercury pollution.
Acting on such suggestions can do more to solve the problem and help the native peoples than all the government's pious platitudes, past programs, and readings from government press releases. It is not good enough for government members merely to talk. The problem is there. It is the result of government inaction. I call on the members of this House and the people of Canada to make sure action is taken to save the health and livelihood of the natives of Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves, and of other areas of Canada which are affected by such pollution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to inform- hon. members that if the Minister of Environment, the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand), cannot be present in the House this afternoon to hear and take part in this debate, it is unfortunately because-and he apologizes-he had to fulfil a commitment he undertook some time ago. Of course he tried to cancel it but it was impossible, and I ask you to accept his apology. He asked me to take part in the debate and to make note of the representations and opinions expressed by the various members so that we can discuss the matter next week. And I can assure you that his officers will carefully examine hon. members' comments.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that although the government's colleagues and critics seemed to indicate that the cabinet was not worrying enough about this environmental problem and about the damages that pollution may cause in many fields, particularly the one to which today's motion is addressed, mercury. I must say that the federal government and the cabinet, and I am sure that applies also to all my colleagues on this side of the House, are very concerned about the problems of pollution. The Department of the Environment employs the most scientists, and they have been working regularly for several years at analysing all causes and effects of pollution. It suggests to the government and its various departments the actions and the precautions that it should take to put a stop to the pollution which has happened throughout the years because of a lack of foresight and also maybe a lack of knowledge. It is particularly important to prevent this pollution from continuing and to reject new formulas or technologies which could endanger the environment.
Of course, it is easy to criticize. However, it is not so easy to apply solutions which take into account not only pollution, but also several economic factors. I would like to congratulate the hon. member who proposed the motion now before the House since it allows the House, of course, but also members of the press, through the information media, to make the population more aware of the need that governments must now face, the need for the population to support and understand the action that all levels of government must take to solve the problem of the environment.
It is not always easy to impose measures to fight and prevent pollution because these measures often restrict freedom and increase business installation costs. Also in
Mercury Poisoning
many cases, and I am now talking as minister responsible for Regional Economic Expansion, several industrial business construction or expansion projects are postponed for a long period and even abandoned because estimated costs to meet the requirements that we now impose on industries are such that the profitability of the business is placed in jeopardy. Naturally, businesses must then postpone their project.
I think it is normal to stiffen requirements in this area, and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has become more and more demanding in the last few years, and each time we are in doubt about an application, we refer it to the Department of the Environment so that it can make a recommendation on the proposed investment. This delays the examination of applications and I even receive criticisms from promoters on the one hand, and representations from my colleagues in the House on the other hand asking me why we delay so much in making the decision. Because of this analysis process concerning all the implications of a particular study we must sometimes delay our decision.
Mr. Speaker, in the 60s some very complex environmental problems imputable to mercury appeared in Japan and Sweden. This prompted environment experts in Canada to launch in 1969-70 a national inventory of mercury uses and its risk for the environment.
As there was a possibility of contamination of mercury treated seeds, the experts started a North American wildlife study. Following that research and particularly the study by the Canadian Wildlife Service, Agriculture Canada prohibited the use of mercury based longicides in 1970-71 under the terms of the Pest Control Products Act.
By the end of 1969, after serious warnings concerning the incidious mercury pollutions in the central provinces, the Fisheries Research Board of Canada launched studies aimed at controlling the contamination level of fish. Several takes of fish from Lake Winnipeg, Saskatchewan River, Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie contained up to nine parts per million of mercury, which instigated the provincial authorities on the advice of the federal department of fisheries and forests to close several commercial fishing zones throughout Canada. At the same time, provincial governments made rod fishermen aware of the risk inherent in eating fish from some areas. On the other hand, the efforts aimed at preventing a high consumption of contaminated fish among the local population was not a complete success.
As is was already recognized in Sweden, it was established that mercury contamination came mainly from industrial sources. A good number of pulp and paper mills used mercury derivatives in their process. When the inquiries demonstrated the seriousness of the mercury problem in North America, the pulp and paper industry voluntarily stopped to use mercury cells as early as 1969-70 which eliminated mercury discharges in the environment, except for minimal quantities related to combustible raw materials and chemical products.
The chlor-alkali industry that produced chlorine from mercury cells was also identified as major source of contamination In December 1970, the federal Minister of the

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
Environment asked that industry to reduce voluntarily its mercury wastes, while legislation was being drafted. Generally speaking, the industry co-operated and the mercury discharged in liquid from, estimated at almost 148,000 pounds a year in 1970 went down to about 6,000 pounds annually as early as in 1971, and to 800 pounds a year over the period from 1973 to 1976.
In March 1972, Mr. Speaker, Environment Canada edict-ed regulations on mercury waste from chlor-alkali plants. Under the Fisheries Act, those regulations limit the quantity of mercury the plants can discharge into the receiving waters. Taking into account the technique available to the industry, the maximum rate of discharge of 1 millionth part of mercury for each ton of chlorine produced has been set as the standard. Since May 1972, all chlor-alkali plants file daily reports on their discharges, as well as their purchases of mercury, regardless of what use it made of it.
Over that period, Environment Canada officials have met the representatives of several companies to discuss their mercury control programs and their compliance to the requirements. In addition, the plants have been supervised by provincial authorities or staff members of the Department of the Environment in order to check the data they have supplied.
According to the files of the department, direct discharges of mercury into water streams have been reduced to a level corresponding to about 1 per cent of that at the time the problem was discovered. Those files have also demonstrated that the total consumption of mercury by chlor-alkali plants is only about half what it was before 1970.
In spite of that substantial reduction, we consider the present consumption as being much too high. The plants have been unable to provide a complete report on their mercury consumption. This summer environment Canada expects to table regulations establishing mercury discharge standards for chlor-alkali plants under the Clean Air Act. The discharge of mercury in the atmosphere by chlor-alkali plants using mercury cells have been estimated at 26.4 tons in 1970 and at 12 tons in 1975. It should be reduced at 2 tons yearly as a result of the application of new measures against air pollution.
We are also trying to find a solution to dispose of dirt and solid wastes from chlor-alkali plants. The most widely used procedures are burying and filling up, but there is also a mecury recovery procedure used by a small number of Canadian plants. We are convinced that regulation and procedures for mercury recovery will reduce mercury use and provide a better control.
In 1973, the CIL plant in Hamilton and the Dow plant in Thunder Bay closed down, and the two Dow plants in Sarnia have phased out their mercury cell system and switched to the diaphragm cell which does not use mercury. In 1975, the mercury cell euipped Reed Paper Company plant in Dryden began using the diaphragm cell without mercury. With the implementation of regulations establishing mercury emission standards for chlor-alkali plants, the old plants will have to convert gradually from mercury cell to non-mercury systems.

Of course, we are aware of the other mercury contaminating sources, such as municipal sources, resistant paints, electric appliances, batteries, as well as mercury emanations from foundries and coal combustion. Added to this industrial contamination is the mercury from natural sources which is found in movement in our waters. The department is carefully monitoring and assessing the mercury from those sources. In addition, it has been evaluating the mercury content in sediments, water, fish and wildlife in order to determine the trends and locate the areas where the problem is serious.
As a result of the steps taken by the industry and the government, I am glad to announce to the House, and I think we will all agree on this, that the situation is improving. A report to be made public shortly by the department shows that the mercury concentration in the waters of western Canada has decreased considerably in the early 70s. The improvement in the west are apparently due mainly to the regulations applicable to chlor-alkali plants, the prohibition of mercury-treatment for grain and the application of purification measures in the industry as a whole. Several areas which had been closed to commercial fishing have been reopened or show signs of reduction of the mercury content of the fish or other forms of aquatic life. Most of the sediments recently formed in the areas affected contain less mercury than those formed at the end of the 60s.
As a matter of fact, the programs of the department have been reasonably successful and markedly reduced the loss of mercury in the aquatic environment. However there are still mercury residues in sediments, mostly downstream from former industrial sources. Unfortunately, these residues will continue to contaminate water bodies and fish for many long years to come. To a large extent, human history is made up of a series of innovations to solve problems. Faced with a challenge, we react by solving the problem and by exploiting its solution. But now, we know the answers. We find that a great number of solutions we adopted have merely served to create further problems, often very serious, and we meet these problems in a great many endeavours of human activity. Regardless of the environment or other problems, our pas conduct comes back to haunt our future.
What we must do, both as individuals and as a society, is to learn to see beyond the immediate advantages derived from our actions, to learn to consider secondary and tertiary, and even more remote consequences. Of course, it is always difficult to evaluate. I know that it is not easy. However, we cannot afford to let immediate advantages outweigh long-term considerations. Too often decisions and measures have been made according to their primary consequences, namely the immediate benefits. These consequences often lead to a chain reaction of prolonged secondary and tertiary and even more remote effects and their public impact can neutralize the initial advantage.
Unfortunately, we have always taken so much time to discover or to determine the long-term effects that to a certain extent we have become the slaves of the immediate advantages and that we have integrated them in our culture. Thus, even before the obviousness of disastrous effects in the long run, it is sometimes hard for us to admit that our original decision was wrong and to try to find an
May 7, 1976

alternative. On the contrary, sometimes we remain fascinated by the short-term advantages and we try to make the system more sophisticated to prevent its long-term effects, as far as possible. It is obvious that we should be more careful, more rational while making our decision. We must look beyond the immediate benefits and attempt to assess the long-term effects. This choice will allways be hard to make.
In the environment area, we have begun changing the way we make decisions. It may be in the environment that the effects of short-term decisions were most evident. Several past benefits are becoming problems now-something we have learned not so long ago. Thus it was only in the late 60s that the results of our actions appeared, both for the planet and for ourselves. From then on, we started to progress, to make better decisions.
The first step was to meet immediate needs. Knowing the effect and the nature of air, earth and water pollution, our natural reaction was to take immediate steps to avoid and, if possible, repair the damage. To do so, we issued various standards and instructions governing the quality of environment and we also regulated some known detrimental operations. It was also the onset of a new technology to control the polluting elements at discharge.
It goes without saying that this approach, though valid, is not sufficient. We must undertake a second stage, prevention, and this is what we are now doing. We are now learning to assess the long term implications of our actions, the real future costs. This is extremely important, not only for the quality of our life, but for our very survival.
Both to set the pace and to increase its knowledge, the federal government through the Department of Environment has established an environmental assessment and review process for ongoing projects of which it is part and which are likely to affect the environment. Not only does the value of such a process lie in the progress which may stem from it but also in the fact that it is a first step towards a valuable consideration of the consequences of our actions.
It is obvious that this process is still in the early stages but it v/orks. Its real value will depend on the way it will prompt others to adopt similar assessment mechanisms with regard to the environment and other realms of human activity. Rational decision making is being impeded whenever we do not have the necessary knowledge to proceed with valuable pre-assessments. For instance, we do not possess sufficient knowledge to delineate the border line between what is a hazard and what is not. We must always take costs and benefits into consideration.
Some people are against the use of aspirin, even if it has been easing the pain of many people for quite a number of years, and it will very unlikely be withdrawn from the market because of the pernicious effects it may have on a very small minority. D.D.T. is accepted by the body under a certain level, even if it can be dangerous for human beings as well as for other living organisms. But, if the use of D.D.T. had been forbidden 30 years ago because of its dangers, millions of people would have died in the meantime from certain diseases, and probably from hunger.
Mercury Poisoning
When we are unduly concerned over the unfavourable effects of a particular thing, we might forget about interesting innovations. So we must decide whether what we get from preventing some technological damage is more important than what we lose if we stop all progress. Mr. Speaker, the answer to this problem is, of course, research. If we agree that evaluations are essential, if we want to take the right decisions, we must be prepared to study very carefully the impact of each alternative.
Another very heavy constraint in this country is that of constitutional jurisdictions. The Canadian political system constitutes in fact a mosaic of various jurisdictions that often paralize us, or at least slow down decisions and action. To speak more clearly, in certain areas of activity decisions and actions by an administrative level have an important effect on others. This is particularly true in the area of environment. One of the annoying characteristics of agreements in that respect is the following: people coming under a particular administration tend to think that the outside harmful effects of their actions do not concern them. That is untrue, of course. We cannot allow jurisdictional limits to restrict the assessment of our actions. This would be abdicating our responsibilities.
Intergovernmental cooperation is a basic must in carrying out the urgent tasks of environmental management. Without that cooperation no political or institutional structure and no distribution of power and responsibility can work. So the essential key to success in managing tomorrow's environment is in short enlightened cooperation based on knowledge and respect for the respective roles of the various levels of government. The notion of development in harmony with nature is based on the application of ecological principles not only with respect to industrial activity but also all our institutions and our culture. Ecology, the science of system indivisibility and interdependence, requires a form of reasoning common to several disciplines and behaviour based on intercommunication. So there is place for symbiotic relationship between individuals, institutions, regions and states. We all know the interaction that exists within our ecosystem and, consequently, we can understand the overall meaning of the term "development in harmony with nature."
We want to elaborate a conceptual representation designed to promote development in harmony with nature in Canada. The basic concepts reside in the fact that ecological principles must permeate the essence of social institutions, culture, the lifestyle and industrial activities designed to provide the goods indispensable to survival. But if those concepts are to continue to exist, develop and take a concrete form, we must solve the main conflicts of national priorities.
Therefore we shall have to develop a social justice and live within the confines of restraints imposed by our environment. This is a fundamental duty: growth in harmony with nature must neither sacrifice the present for the benefit of the future nor the future for the benefit of the present. We must rather apply the wisdom of environmental principles to the development of social institutions, of a life generating system and of ways of livelihood. Mr. Speaker, we are all very aware-and I think Canadians are becoming ever more aware-of the importance of protecting our environment, but we must remember at the same

Mercury Poisoning
time that all governments and all Canadians are also willing to continue to have a standard of living, a quality of life which is among the highest in the world. This is why in this statement I emphasize this challenge, with which we are faced now, of properly assessing the impact of decisions we have to take both on the environment and the quality of life, the standard of living, indeed on incomes and our national economy as a whole.
It is always difficult to decide when confronted with such dilemmas. When a major industrial development is planned in an area or a province, or in the country, and that the economic benefits for the country and the area concerned are being considered, the effects it will have on the environment as a whole must also be weighed. It is always difficult to make a choice. Canadians, I think, can be assured that the present government will do its best to ensure that industries and various governmental agencies take all precautions so that industrial or other developments be carried out with maximum respect for the environment. And if we have no other choice, if it is obvious that the environment must substantially suffer from investments or the growth of an industry, the government will then have to make the difficult choice and refuse that such investment be made in the hope that they can be made in other areas which are equally productive, and which will naturally make a contribution to the economy, while respecting environmental requirements.
I thank hon. members for their contributions and the views. You will understand that I do not necessarily accept all the criticisms that have been voiced because I believe they were overstated in some cases, but on thing is obvious-today's debate, our exchanges of views will most probably contribute to promote the cause of environmental protection as a whole.
