speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), for moving this important motion today in which he censures the government for the shocking neglect of the problem caused by mercury poisoning. Frankly, as a member of parliament I am ashamed how little this issue has been raised in the House of Commons, and as a Canadian I am angered by the apparent low priority that the government places on the well-being of other Canadians whose health and lives are in imminent jeopardy.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the comments of the two government members who have spoken so far. I could not help but feel a little sorry for the role in which the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) has been cast. He is a colleague and friend of mine, and I have a high regard for him. I think he came to parliament out of a great sense of human concern for people in this country, and I am sorry to see him cast in the role of an apologist for the government in which he is required to rehash old government news releases, periodically injecting scientific jargon into them.
I was not, however, so surprised by the minister's performance. If the translator translated what he had to say correctly, he explained it was his responsibility today

to make excuses-that is the word the translator used-for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand) who could be with us today. Certainly making excuses is precisely what the minister did.
The minister says that the Minister of the Environment had other appointments which he could not break, that he had a responsibility to attend them and that he could not be with us here though he would have liked to be. If the minister says that is the case, I accept it. But where is the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), and where is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan)? Surely their stake in this is every bit as great as that of the Minister of the Environment? I am appalled that when an issue like this, which comes before parliament so infrequently, is raised the ministry is able to put up only one minister to speak in the debate, a minister who has no direct jurisdiction in the matter and whose role is to act as an apologist for the government.
Listening to the government spokesman one would feel, if one believed everything that was said, that either there really is not all that much of a problem, or that it will go away by itself, or with the assistance of the great initiatives that have been taken by the government. Frankly it rings a bell in my mind, in fact it was rung this morning when my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent quoted a speech of the Hon. Jack Davis when he was the minister of the environment. This was the quotation that my colleague read, and I would ask other members of the House of Commons to compare this statement with statements that have been made by government apologists so far. He said:
Fortunately we have caught our mercury problem in time. We have caught it before there has been any real danger to human beings. Once spotted, we have closed the fishery. Either that or we have bought up all the fish and had them destroyed. Nothing has escaped the watchful eye of our federal inspection service, a service which is regarded the world over as tops.
Mr. Davis may be gone, but his speech writer lives on. We have been able to see today that he is still well employed in the ministry and certainly has contributed a great deal to the speeches made by members on the government side so far.
Other members on this side have or will be dealing with the health, Indian affairs, environmental and fisheries aspects of this serious problem. In my remarks I will try to address myself primarily to the jurisdictional considerations in order to establish that the federal government has now, and it has had for some years, all the constitutional and legislative authority it needs to deal with mercury pollution. Sadly, what it does not have is the will to do so.
Before considering this question of jurisdiction, however, perhaps in order to bring the effects of federal neglect into sharper focus I should briefly describe the effects of mercury poisoning upon human beings. Dangerously high levels of mercury contamination have been found in the blood of a number of people in northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec, and the early symptoms of mercury poisoning have already become apparent in some of them. Early symptoms of mercury poisoning include a numbness and tingling of the mouth, tongue and limbs, with the accompaniment of tunnel vision. A
May 7, 1976

Minamata disease victim experiences an inability to concentrate, an inarticulate manner, long periods of apathy, extreme fatigue, and emotional instability. The eventual outcome of this disease is the disfigurement of the body and finally death.
Resistance to mercury poisoning is greatest among strong adults, and while a pregnant woman may show no signs of mercury poisoning herself, she can pass high concentrations of mercury into her child within the womb. The newborn infant may show symptons of mercury poisoning. The symptoms include mental retardation and a condition similar to cerebral palsy.
The effects of mercury poisoning are progressive and irreversible. There is no room for error. The government must take a realistic and comprehensive look at this matter, or suffer the moral consequences of its inaction.
It is with a deep sense of regret that I, along with my colleagues, feel compelled to rise in the House today in order to chastise the government for what can only be described as an irresponsible and shortsighted mishandling of the mercury pollution problem which prevails in many of our country's inland waters. My investigation into the mercury pollution problem of this nation has revealed a shocking sense of complacency within the federal bureaucracy.
Government officials are anxious to convey to the public the impression that everything possible is being done in the federal realm to solve this problem. I regret to say that this is not the case. Although the government, at least since 1970, has been aware of heavy metal contamination in the Wabigoon-English River system, six years of discussion and testing have revealed that it has abdicated its moral and constitutional responsibility to effect a quick solution to this problem.
The federal government has skillfully used the principle of provincial property rights as a "catch-22" clause to free itself from responsibility in the cleanup of contaminated waters.
To date the government has been successful in leaving the impression that environmental concerns relating to the pollution of our nation's waters lie almost solely within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. When my office questioned Ontario environmental officials about the apparent jurisdictional problems between the province and the federal government, their reply was that no jurisdictional problem exists.
While provinces own the watersheds within their boundaries and exercise their jurisprudence with respect to property, the province of Ontario administers only the provisions for testing and reporting contained within the federal Fisheries Act and does not enforce that act's prohibitions and sanctions. Enforcement of that part of the Fisheries Act lies within the auspices of the federal government.
Present federal involvement in the area of mercury pollution includes the efforts of a number of government departments. The Department of the Environment has formulated chlor-alkali regulations for industry and conducts an inspection service for all fish products marketed in
Mercury Poisoning
Canada. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development exercises its jurisdiction over Indians on reservations by assisting projects intended to provide alternative employment opportunities for Indians dislodged from the fishing industry following the ban on commercial fishing along the Wabigoon-English River system. The Department of National Health and Welfare is monitoring mercury levels in natives of northwestern Ontario and Quebec, and is providing an education program to persuade Indians not to consume contaminated fish. Beyond these activities, the prevailing Ottawa attitude seems to be that further initiatives to clean up the problem must come from provincial quarters.
Federal footdragging in the area of mercury pollution is difficult to understand when one considers the long history of federal interest in the well-being of Canadian fisheries. One of the first pieces of legislation passed by the federal government in 1867 was the Fisheries Act. Section 91(12) of the British North America Act awards the federal government jurisdiction over seacoast and inland fisheries and gives it the competence to legislate in respect of pollution of waters in so far as pollutants adversely affect the fisheries. The anti-pollution provisions of the act were revised in 1970 to prohibit the deposit of, to use the words of the act, "deleterious substances" in any water frequented by fish or in any place where deposits may enter the water except as authorized. Under the provisions of this act the federal government may exercise its authority to establish national water pollution standards. In 1972 the Department of the Environment established national chlor-alkali standards for industry.
Both my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, and I have read from the address which the Hon. Jack Davis, former Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, made to the Canadian Manufacturer's Association in 1970. Perhaps I could refer to that again. In that address he solicited support from the Canadian public for amendments to the Fisheries Act which pertained to water pollution. The minister declared:
The polluter must pay ... the industry which caused the problem must solve the problem. It must not only improve its housekeeping but also make amends for sloppy practices in the past. It must clean up its operation and it must compensate others who have been hurt by its negligence.
The Fisheries Act amendments have been in place since 1970, yet what has happened to the promise of federal action? The water resources of both the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba, in the case of the Wabigoon-English River system, were contaminated by effluent traced to the Dryden Paper Company's chlor-alkali plant in Ontario.
The Manitoba government has attempted to prosecute the Dryden plant under Manitoba law, and the Supreme Court has declared this unconstitutional. The fact that the Manitoba government failed in its attempt to prosecute the Dryden Paper Company for damage to Manitoba waters in the recent Supreme Court decision clearly reveals that the federal government must take responsibility for the problem. Yet no charges have been laid against the Dryden plant as provided for under the Fisheries Act, despite the fact that federal authorities clearly have the jurisdiction to do so. It seems that this tired Liberal administration is more prone to rhetoric than to action.
13316

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
My office has enquired to ascertain why no charges have been laid to date. I am sure many members of this House would be interested to learn the reason. Frankly, the bureaucrats could not supply the answer. As a matter of fact the Department of the Environment did not seem to have many answers to supply about anything.
During my period of investigation into this matter the director of the water pollution control directorate was unavailable for comment as he was out of town upgrading his facility in Canada's two official languages and he will not be available for another six months. The director's assistant was unavailable as well as he was out of town attending a conference and would not be back for a couple of weeks. The assistant's assistant was likewise not in his office. Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I now harbour grave suspicions that the Department of the Environment comprises only a contingent of embarrassed receptionists. There can be little wonder why the government seems to resemble a rudderless ship.
Does the government not take the plight of Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserve Indians seriously? The government of Japan takes the problem of mercury poisoning very seriously. On Wednesday it was reported that two businessmen from the Chisso Corporation at Minamata were charged with the involuntary manslaughter of seven people who died of mercury poisoning.
In Canada, Section 176 of the Criminal Code may be employed where it is established that a common nuisance has caused physical injury to any person or has endangered the life, safety or health of the public. While it is not necessary to prosecute offenders at Dryden under the Criminal Code, it is essential that the government's conspicuous jurisdictional dodging be resolved.
Mercury pollution is a national problem. It has had its effects felt in at least nine of ten provinces and the territories. Witnesses testifying before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on April 8 professed that mercury pollution is a growing international problem. Recent scientific studies conducted on the Greenland glacial fields indicated mercury pollution is a by-product of the world's growing industrialism. It is a long-term problem.
Canada has more to lose from unchecked mercury pollution than almost any other western nation. The Grassy Narrows and White Dog experience has vividly underlined the social and economic consequences of mercury pollution for our native people whose social structure is built upon a fish economy.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has displayed a shocking lack of leadership with regard to his handling of the problems at the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves. Although section 91(24) of the British North America Act places the well-being of Indians on reservations within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been anxious to push his responsibilities on to other ministers. The minister has taken a very narrow view of this problem. This side of the House is not satisfied with the minister's makeshift solutions and evasions.

Along the Wabigoon-English River system many Indians are continuing to eat contaminated fish because the Indians doubt the sincerity of the government and because they really have little alternative. Thought must be given to moving the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves to a non-contaminated area if consumption of contaminated fish continues. To date, none of the minister's officials have proposed this possibility to the natives.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has a responsibility to Canada's northern peoples to demonstrate some concern and to urge his colleagues to cease their jurisdictional juggling. A great deal of research is needed to conduct further studies on all aspects of mercury pollution. The federal government must arm itself with expertise so that it may also deal with mercury poisoning in the international context. I understand environment Canada is currently conducting an internal task force examination to determine future research and development needs to deal with the mercury pollution problem. The federal government must co-ordinate and catalogue a national effort to gain the knowledge to deal with our mercury pollution problems.
The immense human and economic problems caused by mercury poisoning in Canada are clear. What is distressing is that the government's concern is not. Where there should have been action, there has been paralysis. Where there should have been explanations, there has been silence. And where there should have been basic concern for the health and lives of human beings, there has been indifference.
There is much about life in government which I have found challenging and stimulating, but I have also noticed that the day-to-day atmosphere of crisis here in Ottawa can distort a person's perspective and dull his sense of outrage at attitudes, policies, and actions that would offend deeply the average citizen. After a few years in this environment it becomes easy to view human tragedies as case histories, and human beings as simple statistics. We have heard that happen today.
I fear that it is that desensitization that has struck both parliament and the whole of the federal structure when it comes to mercury poisoning of human beings. That is the reason why the issue has come before parliament so few times, and it is an indictment of this institution that so little has been said about it in this Chamber.
The people of Canada are not indifferent to the human tragedies in northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec. They cannot understand and they will not tolerate the jurisdictional buck-passing that has taken place between federal and provincial authorities. The federal government has today-and it has had for years-all the jurisdiction it needs to deal with this problem. What Canadians from one coast of this country to another demand is that the government use that jurisdiction and act now before more damage is done.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) has brought this matter before the House. While I disagree with some of the statements he made I think it is an excellent proposition to have such a subject brought before the House hopefully for a rational debate
May 7, 1976

rather than one full of sound and fury. It should be a debate not of condemnation but of rationale, because I am sure it is the intent of the House not to say that someone did something right or that someone did something wrong but that we are at a certain point in time, and let us go forward from this point.
The dangers of mercury contamination of the environment were first brought to the public's attention by two major tragedies in Japan in the late 1960's, one of which was instrumental in giving the effects of mercury contamination in the human body the name Minimata disease. Since this time the dangers and effects of this type of environmental irresponsibility have been extensively reported.
Canadian experience in this regard began with the dumping, between 1961 and 1970, of a considerable amount of mercury into the English-Wabigoon river system by the chlor-alkali plant of the Reed Paper Company in Dryden, Ontario. This matter is of concern to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development because of the presence on the English-Wabigoon river system, and downstream from the Reed Paper Mill in Dryden, of two Indian reserves. These are the Grassy Narrows and Whitedog reserves. The concern of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in this regard was not expressed only in relation to the dangers posed to the health of the residents of these reserves, whose population now totals 916. It was also over the threat that the consequences of the mercury contamination of the English-Wabigoon river system would totally destroy the social and economic fabric of the Grassy Narrows-Whitedog Region.
Once the possibility of mercury contamination had been raised, the government of the province of Ontario in light of the dangers of this dumping practice, as evidenced in Japan, investigated and found that the levels of mercury in fish in the English-Wabigoon river system was some twenty times greater than the maximum safe level for human consumption. In 1970, therefore, the effluent from the Dryden mill was reduced by provincial order, commercial fishing in the English-Wabigoon river system was banned, and tests were conducted on residents of both the Whitedog and Grassy Narrows reserves in order to determine the affect on the inhabitants of the mercury contamination. The steps which have been taken to investigate and treat the effects of mercury contamination on the native population of the Dryden area were taken by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of National Health and Welfare, which on behalf of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is providing health care to the Indian population of the Dryden area, the Department of the Environment, and the appropriate departments of the government of the province of Ontario. Indian Affairs has, however, played a much more direct role in helping the residents of Whitedog and Grassy Narrows overcome the tragic effects of the mercury contamination on their economic and social traditions.
I welcome the fact that members on the other side have brought up the matter of the social and economic disruption, because in addition to being a health problem it is also an economic and social problem.
Mercury Poisoning
The mercury contamination, quite simply, kicked the props out from under the entire way of life of these people. Because of the high contamination levels in the local fish, all commercial fishing which had previously been one of the main occupations was halted. In addition, some of the guiding and tourist businesses on the English-Wabigoon river system closed their doors which have not opened since. The result was severe unemployment and severe dislocation in respect of the lives of these people. At Grassy Narrows, for instance, there are 78 employable males. However, after the collapse of the fishing and tourist industries, only 14 band members, or 18% of the total male labour force, had year-round employment. At Whitedog, the situation was worse. Equally tragic was the fact that the traditional food supply of the Whitedog and Grassy Narrows reserves was fish, the same contaminated fish from the same contaminated river system.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, ever since this tragedy was first revealed, has worked hard on behalf of both the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves, and although the situation is still a most serious one-and, Mr. Speaker, I will not make apologies for the fact that it is a serious one, because it is and I will say so-considerable progress has been made.
With respect to the problem of providing an alternate food supply, several important steps have been taken. In conjunction with other departments, an educational program is being carried out to warn the band members not to eat fish from the contaminated rivers. The program includes letters to heads of household, and visit to all houses to discuss this problem on a one to one basis. I am sorry the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) is not present because he indicated, I am sure with no malicious intent-

The development of a suitable Ojibway language audio-visual explanation program has been carried out, as well as the preparation of a 15 minutes videotape film in the Ojibway language. The department has also worked to identify lakes which are free from contamination and which can be safely fished for food, as has been mentioned, and has provided community freezers to the reserves for the storage of mercury free fish which is caught, and also for the storage of fish which being trucked in from other areas by the Ontario government.
I would also like to point out to hon. members that the recent trip by five Indians from the Dryden area along with their advisers to Minamata, Japan, was financed by the federal government, with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the Department of the Secretary of State all sharing the cost. This trip, despite the rather sensational coverage by the media, was a very important and very effective educational session and, I believe, has resulted in a much better understanding of the causes and effects of Minamata's disease on the native people in the area concerned.
I also noted that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie asked that the government take part in a five or six part program, one part of which was to be an exchange program with the Japanese. This has already been started, with the hope that the people in the affected areas will realize the dangers resulting from the eating of contaminated fish, and we hope this will be of some benefit to them.
I would also like to point out that it is not enough just to resolve the problems which have been created. We must also work for the future and try to restore some form of social and economic stability to this troubled area. This the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is attempting to do through a wide ranging series of projects, both short-term and long-term, to help these people whose employment activities have been drastically curtailed. The fact that the health of these people has been affected must be taken into consideration, as well as their loss of employment opportunities.
In addition to the regular programs for economic development, which are of course available to all Indian bands throughout Canada, a number of specific projects have been initiated by the department to provide shortterm employment for area residents. These include the development of local government administration and the hiring of a community worker for each reserve; work opportunity projects for brush cutting and road clearing and for the construction of docks and sheds for fish gear; tree planting; a school lunch program; a LIP grant for a garbage disposal program; training on the job moneys for such things as counselling and an economic development officer; the installation of water and sewage services for community buildings; and a general reserve clean-up and painting. These and other short-term employment projects have been provided in order to help bridge the gap between the severe socio-economic dislocation caused by the mercury contamination and the coming into effect of programs for more long-term employment opportunities. In all honesty I must deny that no funds were provided for the employment of these people whether on a short-term or a long-term basis.
Two of the proposals for long-term employment opportunities which should be mentioned are the canoe factory and the shoe factories. Ground work has already been laid

for two shoe factories to commence operations on reserves in the Dryden area. One of these will be located in Grassy Narrows. A feasibility study has also been initiated to investigate markets and production cost factors for the possible manufacture of fibreglass canoes, also at Grassy Narrows.
I mentioned earlier that as a result of the mercury contamination only 14 members of the Grassy Narrows band-out of a possible 78 in the male work force-were employed at one point. This figure is now up to 42 persons and is an indication of the extent to which the socio-economic conditions on these reserves have been stabilized. While the department, along with other government departments, does not consider it acceptable, it is an indication of the direction in which employment is progressing on this reserve.
I think that the key factor for all hon. members to recognize is that the one thing we have learned in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is that you cannot come in with programs and dictate to the people in the areas what they should be doing for their well-being. I hope that we have learned that lesson and I think we have, because the only way in which the people of the area will develop into a socio-economic unit with a high employment ratio is as a result of the enthusiasm and sense of pride in their own communities which these people are exhibiting, and which I believe is now building up in these reserves. This will do more than all the assistance we can give them to ensure a stable future for this area. This is now happening and I have every confidence that the initiative and leadership which are now being shown by the Whitedog and Grassy Narrows bands will produce significant results in the months ahead.
Before closing I would like to discuss briefly the problem of mercury contamination as it relates to northwestern Quebec. The discovery of mercury contamination in this area from both natural and industrial sources has raised concern for the safety of the Indian bands in the area. In response to this an educational program sponsored by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on the dangers of eating mercury contaminated fish is being carried out. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and the Department of National Health and Welfare are in the process of intensifying the dissemination of information related to mercury poisoning through the use of appropriate audio-visual material, band meetings, and seminars for community leaders and health workers. A joint nutrition committee is also being established by the two departments to research the most appropriate proteins to replace the contaminated fish.
The mercury contamination problem in northwestern Quebec is made more difficult, I am afraid, by natural levels of mercury in the waters of certain lakes and rivers, and also by the more nomadic way of life of the residents of the area as compared to the Indian of northwestern Ontario, as has been mentioned by one hon. member. However, the department is now carrying out a survey of the local labour force, educational levels, and skills acquired so that band councils, with the support of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, can plan and develop adequate and realistic solutions to the health,
May 7, 1976

social, and economic problems created by this tragic legacy of our modern industrial development.
I thank the hon. member for Lambton-Kent for having brought up this subject on an opposition day. I trust that we are realistic enough to realize that in the very complex society in which we live there will be substances which will be toxic and about which we are not aware at this date. I think it is the function of the government as far as possible to try to predict what these substances will be. However, when these matters do arise, surely the government must act with speed and dispatch.
The question raised by the hon. member is whether speed and dispatch have been observed here. When we are dealing with people we cannot go into an area, dictate what they will or will not eat, or what they will or will not do. This is done by a slow process of education and working with them. In that way these problems are solved, and in all sincerity I feel this is the way it has been carried out. This is the way it will be carried out, and I trust that in the future the people in these affected areas will have not only healthy lives but lives of full employment during which they can work as other Canadians, trusting that the approach of the government is the right one. If the solution is a slapdash method of trying to bring in quick relief without having basic studies done, I think that presents as much danger as we are being accused of allowing to exist at the present time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate, and I should first like to congratulate the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) on his very thought provoking address on this issue.
We must ask ourselves, is mercury poisoning Canadians, and will Canadians die of mercury poisoning? I submit that these questions are of increasing concern because mercury can no longer be ignored as a lethal environmental pollutant. These questions demand our attention because some Canadians have blood mercury concentrations within the range associated with mercury poisoning in other countries, notably, Japan and Iraq.
There is no doubt that mercury can kill and maim. During the last two centuries an estimated 8,500 persons have been poisoned by mercury, of whom perhaps 700 died. Mercury poisoning must therefore be considered a hazard to public health wherever mercury is used and wherever mercury is discharged into the environment. This is certainly true for Canada, but so that the entirety of the problem of mercury as an environmental pollutant can be understood, wider aspects of mercury pollution, those relating to Canadian society, must be considered as well. Consider, for example, some of the effects of mercury pollution.
In industry vast quantities of mercury are used in a variety of technological processes. In 1967 world consumption of mercury was 7,364 metric tons, a large proportion of it being used by a few industrial nations. For example, the United States of America used something like 2,127 tons. In Canada chlor-alkali plants, pulp and paper mills and the electrical industry consume much of the total mercury
Mercury Poisoning
used. For example, in 1969 chlor-alkali plants used some 100 of a total of 140 tons required by industry.
With this industrial use large amounts of mercury are discharged into the environment. Of the total of 7,364 tons of mercury consumed by the world in 1967, 2,573 tons were lost to the air and 2,045 tons, it is estimted, were lost to the waterways.
As well as having an effect on health, mercury pollution in Canada has had ecological, socio cultural, political, racial, and international implications. With other factors it has disrupted the lives of Indians and has radically altered their traditional way of life, for the fish on which so many Indians depend for protein have become contaminated with mercury discharged into waterways from chlor-alkali plants and paper and pulp mills. This is particularly serious in northwest Ontario and northwest Quebec. Not surprisingly, the sociological effects of mercury pollution have had a political impact, and federal and provincial authorities have been accused of making light of the dangers of mercury pollution to man and environment in Canada. Nor is it surprising that mercury pollution in Canada has had racial implications, for the Canadians who have the highest mercury concentrations are Canadian Indians.
Finally, there is an international twist. Japanese victims of mercury poisoning have allied themselves with Canadian Indians of northwest Ontario, as have Japanese environmentalists, in an attempt to help Canadian Indians bring their plight to the attention of the federal government. Japanese physicians with much experience in mercury poisoning have examined Canadian Indians and, convinced of mercury poisoning in these Indians, have taken a stronger line than have Canadian physicians on mercury pollution in Canada. Unfortunately there is as yet no agreement on the clinical diagnosis of mercury poisoning.
Mercury has long fascinated man. It was been dubbed a mineral of a perfectly singular kind. Ramazzini, the father of industrial medicine, spoke in the eighteenth century of the most cruel bane of all that deals death and destruction to miners and of course Lewis Carroll's Mad Hatter lives on as a symbol of the damage done to the nervous system by mercury. The Mad Hatter conjures up an image of poisoning due to inorganic mercury, and this form of mercury poisoning was for long the most familiar. Today, however, because of the burgeoning of sophisticated technological processes, it is poisoning from organic mercury which is of major concern. Methyl mercury in particular damages the central nervous system irreversibly and sometimes fatally. The experience of several countries merits the attention of Canadian professional people.
It was in 1965 that a Japanese factory doctor in Minamata, a small town on the western coast of Kyushu in southern Japan, reported that an unclarified disease of the central nervous system had broken out. Soon, some 30 persons were found to have contracted the disease, now known as Minamata disease, during the previous three years. Diligent investigation finally disclosed that the disease was a disorder of the nervous system caused by poisoning with methyl mercury.
The disorder appeared to affect only fishermen and their
families in and around Minamata. The patients evidently
ate large amounts of fish and shellfish from Minamata Bay

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning
regularly, which were found to contain high concentrations of mercury, of the order of 5 parts to 20 parts per million. The concentration of mercury in the mud of Minamata Bay was related directly to the proximity of the sample tested to a plastics factory in Minamata which produced vinyl chloride, an inorganic mercury compound being used as the catalyst. A similar disorder was produced in cats by feeding them fish contaminated with methyl mercury.
Another outbreak of Minamata disease occurred in Niigata, Japan, in 1964 and 1965. It was virtually identical with the disease which had broken out in Minamata. To December, 1974, 798 persons in Japan had been verified as having Minamata disease, and of these some 107 died.
The Japanese experience is relevant to the Canadian situation because the Canadian Indians, in whom high blood concentrations have been found, are like the Japanese of Minamata, heavy fish eaters, and fish in some Canadian waters have high concentrations of mercury. However, the Japanese data are less useful than those of studies of methyl mercury poisoning elsewhere because blood concentrations apparently were not documented at the time of intoxication.
The experience of Japan and other countries is a useful but disturbing background to the Canadian experience, but the Canadian experience also is disturbing. Vast quantities of mercury have been dumped into Canadian waterways. Between May of 1972 and April of 1975 major chemical companies were unable to account for up to 65 per cent of the mercury purchased. One plant in northwest Quebec lost something like 7,437 of 11,248 tons of mercury during this period.
Evidence of mercury pollution of Canadian waterways has been available since 1969 when the South Saskatchewan and the St. Clair rivers were found to be contaminated. A contaminated river may require up to 70 years to cleanse itself through natural processes, so methyl mercury will persist in Canadian waters for many years to come.
Mercury concentrations in fish in some Canadian waters exceed the federally acceptable upper limit of 5 parts per million. In 1969 concentrations of up to 10 parts per million were reported in fish in the South Saskatchewan River, and since then concentrations several times 5 parts per million have been measured frequently in many Canadian waters.
Canadian Indians, like Japanese fishermen, are heavy fish eaters. If mercury concentrations in the fish eaten by these Indians exceeded one part per million, which has happened on some Indian reservations, the daily safe limit of 0.03 milligrams of methyl mercury will be exceeded.
High whole-blood mercury concentrations in Canadian Indians were first reported in 1970, when the maximum concentration of 385 parts per billion was found in an Indian of the White Dog community in northwestern Ontario. The following year Indians from the northwest Quebec communities of Matagami and Miquelon were found to have abnormally high whole-blood concentrations. Government authorities have been monitoring mercury contamination since 1971, but extremely high concen-

trations were reported as late as July, 1975. Not surprisingly, government authorities have been charged with being indecisive and slow to take action to correct the situation. In part, any indecisiveness of action stems from lack of agreement on what constitutes a positive diagnosis of poisoning.
A further charge directed at federal and provincial authorities concerns a wait-and-see attitude. Public opinion suggests that the policy is to wait until symptoms appear before it is admitted that Canadians are being poisoned by mercury. This attitude also is attributable to lack of agreement on diagnosis, but steps have been taken to reduce further exposure to mercury among the Indians; thus, fishing has been restricted, uncontaminated fish have been supplied to Indians, and extensive monitorings and research have been initiated.
The bulk of Canadians' food supply is, of course, free from hazardous mercury contamination, with some important exceptions. One important area where there is significant mercury contamination has already been referred to, namely, the fish in the English-Wabagoon and Bell river systems of northwestern Ontario and Quebec, which comprise tjie traditional food supplies of the two native groups discussed earlier. Another exception is swordfish, the sale of which in Canada and the United States is still prohibited because the mercury levels are higher than 0.5 parts per million. The published data confirms this point uniformly. An official of Environment Canada stated early in April, 1976, that the mercury levels in swordfish are regularly monitored and that they remain at an average of about 0.9 parts per million. This level has remained unchanged during the past five years. The official further stated that the level was not and is not expected to change, because the mercury in the oceans is from "natural" sources, as opposed to the preventable mercury pollution which comes from human sources.
The banning of swordfish sales in Canada after 1970 and the simultaneous ban on exports to the United States was especially damaging to my native province, Nova Scotia, whose fishermen caught almost all the swordfish for Canada. Landings alone in 1969 were worth more than $4 million. In a fisheries economy the value of these swordfish when exported was, of course, many times that figure.
In legal and biological terms the situation is quite clear-cut. Swordfish contain, on average, about twice the acceptable level of mercury, and it has been proven that almost all this mercury is present as methyl mercury. Further, there is every indication that this has always been and will always remain the case. In this respect the situation differs subtly from that facing inland fisheries, inasmuch as most of the inland mercury contamination originates from manmade sources. However, because swordfish are contaminated they cannot be sold in Canada. Because the U.S.A. has adopted the same 0.5 parts per million standard, the fish cannot be exported to that country, because U.S. federal law under the Federal Food and Drug Administration controls the importation of fish.
An anomalous situation has arisen in the United States with regard to the sale of swordfish. I point this out because individual states do not have to abide by federal health standards. Some states, namely, Maine and Massa-chussetts, allow their fishermen to sell their swordfish
May 7, 1976

catches within the state. But this fish is banned from inter-state commerce by United States federal law. Needless to say this situation is confusing to fishermen and confusing to observers in Canada, because of the double standard that it creates. However, state actions will have no overt bearing on Canadian sword-fishing, because United States federal law is predominant in matters of import and export.
A second anomaly is present in this situation. While swordfish or any species of fish containing more than 0.5 parts per million of mercury is not acceptable for sale in Canada, such fish can be exported to other countries, provided the importing country's standards of health protection allow the importation. Thus Nova Scotia fishermen may be free to export their swordfish catch to Japan, which apparently has a higher acceptable contamination level-an ironic situation, considering the Japanese experience at Minamata and Niigata. However, fisheries officials have stated that the Japanese, who catch their own swordfish off Japan, are willing to pay only about 25 cents per pound for Canadian swordfish, or about half the prices needed by our fishermen to make the venture economically viable.
When we consider that the known levels of mercury in swordfish are not greatly in excess of tolerable levels, it seems to me that some research should be undertaken to lower the mercury content in swordfish. This could be done through different processing methods. It seems to me that, as the world's population grows and there is a continuing demand for protein, some method must be found to use these fish which, landed, weigh anywhere between 25 pounds and as much as 500 pounds; it could be done by mixing the flesh of these fish with that of other, smaller fish which contain lower amounts of mercury. By doing this the mercury content could be brought down to the tolerable limit of five parts per million. Actually, this process is now taking place in the tuna industry.
Tuna containing mercury levels in excess of five parts per million are mixed with the smaller Bonita tuna, and the mixed fish is marketed as flaked tuna. There is nothing wrong with flaked tuna, and its mercury content does not exceed the tolerable limit of five parts per million. This process which may be examined by the fishing industry, government, and scientists gives us hope that, in future, the delectable swordfish may be processed in the same manner.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the question of whether some Canadians are being poisoned by mercury is not easy to answer, but there is sufficient evidence that methyl mercury is harmful and that some Canadians do have unacceptably high whole-blood concentrations of mercury. Because of the sinister possibility of mercury-induced irreversible brain damage the current situation demands our full attention. I submit that action is required. What should be done?
Mercury Poisoning
First, the multidepartmental approach to mercury poisoning in Canadians should be replaced by one that is the responsibility of a single group. At present three governments, several government departments, at least one outside consultant, various local authorities, numerous neurologists and many other interested persons have separate responsibility.
In addition, various task forces and conferences on mercury contamination have added to the wealth of information now available on mercury poisoning. What is required is a cohesive effort to synthesize this information and the approaches of the past so that the Indians, the group mainly affected, can be given a clearer indication that a constructive approach will be followed.
Second, still more needs to be learned on the effects of methyl mercury, particularly its subclinical effects. Much of the information we have today is based on outbreaks of mercury poisoning elsewhere, the relevance of which to the situation in Canada is not entirely clear. Much more basic research is required into the problem of dose and response; and more epidemiologic research is needed concerning, for example, the degree to which mercury poisoning is irreversible, and autopsy findings in those known to have been exposed to high mercury whole-blood concentrations.
Third, it is desirable that differences between Canadian and Japanese neurologists, and between Canadian neurologists, be resolved. This will not be easy because these differences stem from differences in interpretation of clinical findings relating to Canadian Indians examined. In part the differences are attributable to a fragmented and quasi-political approach to the problem of mercury poisoning.
Finally, we need a mature philosophical approach to the management of environmental problems, of which mercury contamination is but one. The current approach is a stopgap one, for like so many environmental problems, mercury contamination is just one of many that require solution at any one time, and the solution to any one problem, then, is inadequate. Many of those who are trying to deal with an urgent problem must simultaneously be dealing with others; this is true, for example, of the medical services branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare which is attempting to overcome the difficulties of mercury contamination in Indians while also dealing with many other unrelated matters, despite limitations in personnel and resources.
It is in part a matter of priorities, but to a much greater extent our current problems have a more fundamental origin: Canada lacks the aggressive environmental legislation philosophy of a country like Sweden, which puts teeth into its environmental legislation and muscle into the actions required.
Preventive medicine is always less glamorous than therapeutic medicine. Yet if the health of Canadians is to be preserved, it is issues such as mercury pollution that are likely to be more important in the long run than many other apparently more pressing issues.

May 7, 1976
Mercury Poisoning

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT INACTION IN FINDING SOLUTION TO PROBLEM OF POLLUTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to elaborate on the program presently being undertaken by the Department of National Health and Welfare concerning mercury poisoning.
Mercury poisoning has become a familiar topic with those who read newspapers. Scarcely a week goes by without some new article or some report of a new revelation or finding. Yet a growing recognition of the problem now known as Minamata disease began only in the mid-1960's. Due to this growing awareness, testing was first initiated among the Indian people living on reserves, in areas of known mercury pollution in northwestern Ontario in 1970, and in northwestern Quebec in 1971. It was as a result of the health finding of these tests that the medical services branch of the Department of Health and Welfare undertook an educational campaign to encourage persons in the areas so affected to limit their intake of fish which had been contaminated by mercury.
Since that time, much more information has become increasingly apparent. The Department of Health and Welfare bases its program to combat the problem on the following premises: First, the mercury levels in fish are still hazardous and will remain so for some years; second, damage to health from mercury poisoning. Once it has progressed to this stage it is believed to be irreversible. There is no absolutely sure "safe level" for all individuals. There is, however, uncertainty about the seriousness of the effects of low levels of exposure over a long period of time.
Third, the emphasis must therefore be on prevention of intake of mercury. In practical terms this means that no contaminated fish should be eaten. Fourth, for this reason emphasis is placed on educating people not to eat any contaminated fish at all, rather than simply encouraging them to reduce their intake, and on helping them to adjust to other eating habits. Fifth, this must be accompanied by a health monitoring program which identifies those most at risk and concentrates advices, assistance, and health surveillance on these individuals. This program specifically involves the indentification of those persons at risk by means of blood and/or hair tests. This includes, particularly, fishing guides and their families, and pregnant mothers.
The purpose of such identification is to monitor the progress of such persons at risk in terms of their mercury intake, and therefore their blood mercury levels, and to perform periodic testing of persons at risk in order to ensure that blood mercury levels are, in fact, falling. It involves conducting clinical examinations of persons at risk to determine the presence of disease due to mercury; and conducting a nutritional program to determine first of all to what extent persons in affected areas rely on contaminated fish in their diet and, secondly, to investigate alternative sources of protein, that is, sources which are both available, affordable, and acceptable.
It should be noted that in the course of this nutritional program the safe level of mercury in fish for this particular population already at risk has been redefined at 0.2 parts per million, instead of the present level of 0.5 parts per million generally accepted as safe for those populations not at risk. In addition, the Indian Affairs Branch is advised of any necessary measures that are required for protein replacement in such a program.
Since the initial testing in 1970, the department has been active in some 25 Indian communities. Over 3,000 people have been tested by blood and/or hair sampling. To date the major involvement in this area has been in northwestern Ontario and northwestern Quebec. I should like to deal with each of these areas, northwestern Ontario first.
Since the winter of 1972-73 a yearly health survey has been carried out by the province of Ontario with the support and assistance of this department. Such tests established that blood levels of mercury were not falling. Adequate numbers of persons were not coming forward for testing, and concern was expressed that a survey carried out in winter did not accurately reflect maximum periods of fish intake.
As I am now coming to a complex part, perhaps I might call it five o'clock.
